case_text: A 66-year-old male arrives for evaluation in anticipation of a small-scale operative procedure recommended by his primary clinician to address a nagging concern that has affected his comfort and function. He explains that the upcoming intervention is intended to be carried out through a limited incision, and he has been told it should not require extensive hospitalization. Over the past few weeks, he has been recuperating from an episode of lung inflammation that set in less than a month ago, during which he experienced pronounced coughing fits and occasional bouts of fever necessitating oral antibiotic treatment. Now largely recovered from that respiratory setback, he states that his strength has returned to near baseline, and he has no current issues with breathing or chest discomfort when he lies down, walks short distances, or exerts himself momentarily around the house. He denies a history of newly developing swelling over his ankles or feet, clarifying that he has not struggled with any recent heart-related condition that would leave him feeling tired or breathless when lying flat. On review, the patient is free of an ischemic stroke diagnosed within the last month. He also mentions never having used a cumbersome cast or bulky immobilization device for his arms or legs in the last month, stating that he maintained a reasonable level of movement despite occasionally feeling fatigued during the worst days of his respiratory infection. In regard to substantial surgical interventions, he has not undergone any large-scale operations in the recent past and reports no major invasive procedures within this same interval, apart from scheduling the minor one forthcoming. He denies bone or joint injuries that could have resulted from serious trauma, and he has not experienced any significant event involving the spinal cord that would leave him paralyzed or otherwise severely compromised in terms of function. He also notes no abrupt neurological phenomena such as loss of sensation, sudden speech disturbance, or weakness isolated to one side that might be suggestive of a recent widespread vascular insult in the brain. On examination, his lower legs do not display abnormal swelling, yet he refers to longstanding visibility of twisting superficial vessels in the calves, a feature that sometimes leads to mild discomfort if he stands for lengthy periods. Despite these changes, he has not been diagnosed with any clot formation in the deeper vessels of his legs, nor has he been told that a clot traveled to his lungs at any stage of his medical history. However, when pressed about familial concerns, he admits to at least one close relative who faced a severe circulatory blockage in the past, prompting him to be mindful about blood-related health risks. He further states that he is free from any chronic inflammation in his digestive tract, has never been informed of major cardiac damage from blocked arteries, and has not gone through a malignant process requiring intensive treatment. Currently, he remains able to move around without significant limitation, stands and walks independently during daily tasks, and attributes his readiness to the two-week window of relative rest following his respiratory illness. He affirms that routine blood checks and other preliminary tests have not signaled alarming abnormalities, and he feels that with mild sedation and proper perioperative strategies, he can safely proceed with the planned small operation. Although he harbors some anxiety due to having heard about clotting issues in relatives, he is motivated to correct his current ailment, anticipating minimal downtime after this limited intervention and hoping to return promptly to his usual household chores and recreational interests.

case_text: A 62-year-old male presents for admission and evaluation prior to a planned extensive open operation aimed at addressing residual complications following a significant gastrointestinal procedure he underwent roughly four weeks ago. According to his account, that previous intervention involved a large incision and required several hours in the operating room, as surgeons worked to remove a diseased segment of bowel. Although his immediate postoperative course was generally uneventful, he experienced pronounced fatigue and mild discomfort at the incision site, which prompted careful monitoring. He states that over the past month, he has had regular follow-up appointments where his surgical team assessed his wound healing and overall recovery. He recalls that there were no episodes of large-volume fluid accumulation, major blood flow deficits, or new cardiac symptoms in the intervening weeks. In particular, he denies any episodes of significant breathing difficulty or coughing fits that might point to an infectious process in his lungs. He likewise reports feeling free of systemic inflammatory responses such as marked fever or severe chills. During conversations with his care providers, he explains that he is not aware of having any lasting issues with compromised airway function. He also highlights that he has not needed strong intravenous antibiotics for an overwhelming bloodstream infection during his convalescence, and he has not been reliant on intravenous lines for medication or nutrition outside of a short period immediately after his initial surgery. Regarding his musculoskeletal condition, he denies that he has been immobilized in a hard cast or that he suffered any serious bone breaks in recent memory. He has not encountered high-impact injuries affecting multiple areas of his body, nor has he dealt with sudden neurological deficits or spinal cord problems that could leave him weak or disabled. He further mentions that he has not noticed bulging superficial veins on his legs, nor has he developed tendon or joint complications beyond routine postoperative aching related to his abdominal incision. At no point in his life has he been informed of a clot forming in a deep vessel of the legs, nor has he ever been told he experienced a traveling clot into the lung circulation. When asked about his relatives, he discloses that several of them have struggled with serious blood-flow blockages, prompting health professionals to suggest a broader familial predisposition to undesired clot formation. Despite that family history, he states that his own prior workups for inherited susceptibility markers were unrevealing, with all relevant laboratory assays showing no significant evidence of a particular gene alteration or immune-mediated clotting abnormality. He emphasizes that he has not dealt with chronic bowel inflammatory conditions, nor does he recollect being told of malignant changes or a need for oncology-focused care, despite having regular evaluations for other issues. He denies any long-standing cardiac disease that would compromise his pump function, explaining that no specialist has flagged unusual swelling in his extremities or shortness of breath upon exertion. He also underscores that he is able to walk around the house independently and has maintained the capacity for light exercise, though he admits that his stamina has decreased somewhat while recovering from his last procedure. On examination, he appears alert, with stable vital signs, clear lungs on auscultation, and no signs of fluid overload. His heart rhythm is unremarkable, and there is no peripheral edema in his lower extremities. Looking ahead to the forthcoming major operation, he voices concern about the risks and hopes to optimize his status in anticipation of anesthesia. He expresses determination to follow any medical directives that might reduce the chance of circulatory complications, highlighting that he is eager for relief from the persistent abdominal discomfort and the limitations brought on by his lengthy healing process. Overall, he appears motivated to proceed, and the surgical team plans to admit him for final testing and careful preparation before moving forward with the planned open intervention.

case_text: A 63-year-old male comes to the clinic for a preoperative evaluation in anticipation of a minimally invasive procedure on his knee, which has exhibited recurrent stiffness and discomfort ever since he resumed activity following a substantial abdominal operation he underwent several weeks ago. According to his recollection, the earlier operation required an extensive incision and a prolonged stay in the hospital for monitoring, during which he eventually recovered enough to be discharged home with instructions to gradually increase his physical activity. However, soon after returning home, he developed signs of a recent lung infection manifested by fever, productive coughing, and shortness of breath, ultimately requiring prompt intervention with antimicrobial therapy. He states that once the respiratory symptoms resolved, he attempted to resume a more normal routine, reporting that he feels able to rise from a seated position, walk around his home, and climb short flights of stairs without undue restriction or dependence on assistive devices. Despite this relative return to mobility, he has lately noted swelling in both of his lower extremities, particularly around late afternoon or evening, when the calves appear mildly puffy and retain indentations if pressed with a finger. He emphasizes that he has never before observed this kind of persistent lower-limb swelling and wonders whether his recent prolonged inactivity during hospitalization contributed to fluid retention. He has no history of twisted superficial vessels along his legs, denies any prior blockages in deep veins or breathing issues due to clots traveling to his lungs, and mentions that none of his close relatives have reported significant benefits or injuries related to irregular blood clotting. He likewise acknowledges no history of severe infections in the bloodstream or any widespread injury that would have confined him to bed for an extended period aside from his recent recovery period. With regard to fractures, he underscores that he has not experienced any broken bones in his hips or legs in modern memory, nor has he faced neurological complications leading to sudden paralysis. In discussing other conditions, he states he has never been diagnosed with an ongoing inflammatory disorder affecting his intestines, has not encountered an episode of reduced blood flow to his heart muscle requiring urgent cardiology intervention, and remains free of chronic lung conditions that would necessitate daily inhaled therapies. He also clarifies that he has had no formal diagnosis of any type of tumor or malignancy, and routine health screenings have consistently shown no evidence of suspicious growths. In terms of laboratory findings, he reports that previous assessments have never revealed any abnormalities regarding specific factors involved in thrombosis or unusual markers that might predispose him to bleeding or clot formation, and he has never been advised to discontinue certain medications because of platelet-related complications. On current examination, he appears stable, with normal heart and lung sounds on auscultation and no acute distress, though mild bilateral edema is evident below the knees. He expresses particular concern about this swelling since it is a new development, but he remains intent on proceeding with his planned procedure, which will be carried out via small incisions to visualize and address an ongoing structural issue in the affected knee. Overall, he exhibits optimism that correcting the joint problem through careful surgical intervention will restore more consistent functionality to his leg and, in turn, allow him to better manage daily activities without the setbacks he has faced since his recent hospitalization.

case_text: A 66-year-old male presents for evaluation in anticipation of a minimally invasive joint procedure involving camera guidance and small incisions around his knee. He states that the plan for this operative intervention arose after months of discomfort in his right knee, often aggravated by daily tasks such as climbing stairs or crouching. He reports that, despite his current difficulties with knee pain, he has not undergone any large-scale operations or lengthy hospital-based interventions in recent weeks, attributing his most recent hospital contact only to nonsurgical management after a traumatic event. Approximately one month ago, he experienced a severe accident resulting in sudden loss of movement below the waist, which prompted urgent hospitalization and thorough neurological assessment. According to him, scans revealed significant but not complete damage to the spinal cord, leading to partial lower extremity paralysis that initially confined him to bed rest. Intensive physical therapy was initiated, and over several sessions, he gradually regained most of his motor function, now able to walk without assistive devices, bend at the knees, and independently manage household tasks without substantial limitations. He continues to note occasional sensory deficits and mild weakness in certain muscle groups, yet insists that his day-to-day mobility has largely returned to a level he considers acceptable for routine living activities. While reviewing his past medical history, he adds that he has not been diagnosed with any ongoing or chronic problems involving heart muscle performance or fluid congestion in the lungs, nor has he been troubled by any persistent respiratory infections or chest infiltrates that required acute intervention over the last several weeks. He remembers a few episodes of cough and mild viral illness in the distant past but insists these never led to hospitalized care or prolonged antibiotic use. He further states that he has never been told of breaks or severe injuries to his hips or legs that necessitated immobilizing casts or advanced fixation procedures, underscoring that his recent spinal trauma was distinct in nature and did not involve fracturing bones. He denies having suffered any abrupt neurological loss affecting speech or cognition, explaining that he has never manifested signs typical of a vascular event in the brain. In discussing circulation, he emphasizes that he has not encountered blockages in his lower limbs or in the blood vessels of his lungs, and he recalls no mention of abnormal clots during hospital evaluations. He denies a history of such problems among his close relatives, asserting he is unaware of any significant clotting difficulties that run in his family. Nonetheless, he mentions that, during an evaluation several years ago, basic genetic and laboratory screening revealed no alarming markers. He remarks that no physician has suggested that he might harbor an unusual inherited or acquired predisposition toward blood clots. He says his routine blood counts and chemistries have been unremarkable, and he has never experienced adverse effects from clot-preventing medications. On inspection of his legs, he notes the presence of enlarged superficial vessels in both calves, which have been visible for some time but do not currently cause pain or fluid accumulation. He reports no puffiness or marked edema around his ankles, clarifying that he only has some mild fatigue at the end of a long day. He denies any bowel-related inflammatory disorder, confirming that his gastrointestinal health has been stable, with no recurring abdominal pain or frequent diarrhea that might suggest chronic inflammation in the intestines. He also states that past evaluations never indicated a malignancy or led to therapies specifically targeting a cancerous process, and he has no chronic respiratory ailments requiring inhalers. Clinically, he appears in stable condition, with normal vital signs and a cooperative demeanor, though he occasionally shifts his weight to manage the mild ache stemming from his knee. He is prepared for the upcoming camera-assisted procedure, expressing hope that addressing the mechanical issues in his joint will improve his daily comfort and independence. He trusts that with continued adherence to medical guidance, including physical exercise, he will maintain reliable mobility despite the lingering consequences of his recent spinal trauma. Overall, he remains optimistic that this less extensive operation will not only restore better function to his problematic knee but also facilitate a smoother path back to his preferred level of physical activity.

He reports that, despite his current difficulties with knee pain, he has not undergone any large-scale operations or lengthy hospital-based interventions in recent weeks, attributing his most recent hospital contact only to nonsurgical management after a traumatic event. Approximately one month ago, he experienced a severe accident resulting in sudden loss of movement below the waist, which prompted urgent hospitalization and thorough neurological assessment. According to him, scans revealed significant but not complete damage to the spinal cord, leading to partial lower extremity paralysis that initially confined him to bed rest. Intensive physical therapy was initiated, and over several sessions, he gradually regained most of his motor function, now able to walk without assistive devices, bend at the knees, and independently manage household tasks without substantial limitations. He continues to note occasional sensory deficits and mild weakness in certain muscle groups, yet insists that his day-to-day mobility has largely returned to a level he considers acceptable for routine living activities. While reviewing his past medical history, he adds that he has not been diagnosed with any ongoing or chronic problems involving heart muscle performance or fluid congestion in the lungs, nor has he been troubled by any persistent respiratory infections or chest infiltrates that required acute intervention over the last several weeks. He remembers a few episodes of cough and mild viral illness in the distant past but insists these never led to hospitalized care or prolonged antibiotic use. He further states that he has never been told of breaks or severe injuries to his hips or legs that necessitated immobilizing casts or advanced fixation procedures, underscoring that his recent spinal trauma was distinct in nature and did not involve fracturing bones. He denies having suffered any abrupt neurological loss affecting speech or cognition, explaining that he has never manifested signs typical of a vascular event in the brain. In discussing circulation, he emphasizes that he has not encountered blockages in his lower limbs or in the blood vessels of his lungs, and he recalls no mention of abnormal clots during hospital evaluations. He denies a history of such problems among his close relatives, asserting he is unaware of any significant clotting difficulties that run in his family. Nonetheless, he mentions that, during an evaluation several years ago, basic genetic and laboratory screening revealed no alarming markers. He remarks that no physician has suggested that he might harbor an unusual inherited or acquired predisposition toward blood clots. He says his routine blood counts and chemistries have been unremarkable, and he has never experienced adverse effects from clot-preventing medications. On inspection of his legs, he notes the presence of enlarged superficial vessels in both calves, which have been visible for some time but do not currently cause pain or fluid accumulation. He reports no puffiness or marked edema around his ankles, clarifying that he only has some mild fatigue at the end of a long day. He denies any bowel-related inflammatory disorder, confirming that his gastrointestinal health has been stable, with no recurring abdominal pain or frequent diarrhea that might suggest chronic inflammation in the intestines. He also states that past evaluations never indicated a malignancy or led to therapies specifically targeting a cancerous process, and he has no chronic respiratory ailments requiring inhalers. Clinically, he appears in stable condition, with normal vital signs and a cooperative demeanor, though he occasionally shifts his weight to manage the mild ache stemming from his knee. He is prepared for the upcoming camera-assisted procedure, expressing hope that addressing the mechanical issues in his joint will improve his daily comfort and independence. He trusts that with continued adherence to medical guidance, including physical exercise, he will maintain reliable mobility despite the lingering consequences of his recent spinal trauma. Overall, he remains optimistic that this less extensive operation will not only restore better function to his problematic knee but also facilitate a smoother path back to his preferred level of physical activity.

case_text: A 74-year-old male presents for evaluation in anticipation of a scheduled procedure intended to replace a deteriorating joint in his lower limb, as his orthopedic team has advised that such an operation could significantly improve his pain control and mobility. He reports that, roughly three weeks ago, he underwent a substantial abdominal operation for a separate issue, requiring a brief hospitalization and a structured recovery period. Following discharge from that previous intervention, he notes that his overall condition improved until he experienced an acute neurological episode about two weeks ago, described by him as a sudden onset of left-sided weakness and a transient difficulty with speech. According to his account, those symptoms have since largely resolved, and he has been continuing a mild exercise routine at home to maintain strength in his limbs. He emphasizes that he is now able to walk unassisted around his home and even complete short errands on foot, which reassures him that his baseline function remains close to normal. However, lingering fatigue sometimes slows him, prompting him to proceed cautiously and use rest periods throughout the day. He denies any new significant cardiac or respiratory problems since his recent hospital admissions, remarking that he has not noticed concerning fluid retention, persistent cough, or episodes of feeling breathless that would indicate an emerging cardiopulmonary issue. Over the course of his adult life, he occasionally experienced troublesome gastrointestinal flare-ups for which he was eventually diagnosed with a chronic condition affecting his bowel, and he recounts multiple strategies used in the past to control bouts of abdominal pain and irregular bowel habits. He states that at present, these gastrointestinal symptoms are fairly well controlled, and he has not required emergency evaluations related to that problem for several years. When asked about vascular health and family history, he remarks that his relatives have not reported unusual clotting events, and he himself has never been told that his blood tests showed concerning hereditary factors or autoantibodies implying predisposition to vascular blockages. The patient's father has varicose veins. Additionally, he specifies that no healthcare provider has previously diagnosed him with any irregularities in his veins, such as conspicuous surface-level abnormalities or pockets of fluid accumulation in his legs. He points out that even though he has struggled with knee discomfort for some time, he has never been advised that specialized supportive devices or immobilizing casts were required, and his clinical team has targeted this upcoming procedure as the most definitive way to restore his quality of life. During the interview, the patient underscores that he does not recall any direct trauma to the hip or leg bones recently, nor does he describe any systemic infections in the latest period that might have interfered with his recovery. On the day of evaluation, he appears oriented and cooperative, with stable vital signs and no evident respiratory distress. Physical examination of his lower limbs reveals limited range of motion in the affected joint, although this is not accompanied by swelling or signs of acute inflammation. He appreciates that his ability to move around has fallen short of his usual activity level, yet he still manages his daily household routines without outside assistance. He expresses optimism that once the new joint is in place, his ambulation will improve drastically, allowing him to resume longer walks and potentially engage in light recreational pursuits. While he is aware of the risks associated with an operation of this magnitude, he believes it is necessary given the persistent pain and mechanical difficulties that have compounded over time, particularly after his recent health challenges. Hospital notes confirm that his neurologic recovery is ongoing, and his clinicians plan to monitor him closely in the perioperative stage, especially in regard to ensuring stable circulation and avoiding potential complications. He has already met with nutritional experts to confirm that his diet is suitable for perioperative healing and to address his longstanding gastrointestinal background. As he awaits final approval for the planned joint replacement, the patient maintains a hopeful outlook, believing that careful attention to rehabilitation protocols and compliance with follow-up visits will allow him to emerge from surgery with an enhanced capacity to walk, climb stairs, and handle all the activities of daily life more comfortably.

case_text:
A 78-year-old man diagnosed with sick sinus syndrome received a permanent pacemaker (DDDR-MRI Medtronic [ventricular lead (MEDTRONIC cistofix 5076–58 cm); atrial lead (MEDTRONIC cistofix 5076–52 cm)]). The procedure itself and the post-procedure screening were both uneventful. The wound was clean, and there was no evidence of pneumothorax or hemothorax on the chest X radiography (CXR). The patient was discharged on the second day after the procedure.
However, the patient complained of a productive cough during a routine outpatient clinic follow-up visit conducted a week after the procedure. Laboratory findings showed a decrease in hemoglobin level from 10.9 to 8.9 mg/dL. A CXR revealed newly developed borderline cardiomegaly and bilateral blunting of the diaphragmatic angle. Pacemaker interrogation results showed normal threshold and impedance of both leads. An evaluation performed at fourteen days after the procedure showed evidence of orthopnea, dyspnea upon exertion, and a minor fever (38 °C). Physical examination showed engorgement of the jugular vein, basal crackles over the bilateral lower lung fields, and pitting edema in both legs. Laboratory data revealed worsening anemia (decrease in hemoglobin level from 8.9 to 7.7 mg/dL), high NT-proBNP (1610 pg/ml), and hyponatremia (Na: 115 meq/L, Osmo: 267), but no leukocytosis or worsening of renal function. An echocardiography revealed moderate pericardial effusion (maximal thickness 1.5 cm) without dynamic diastolic collapse of the right ventricle (RV).
The patient was treated for congestion, and administered a nitrate infusion. The patient also received empirical treatment with antibiotics since the low-grade fever was suggestive of an infection. The workup for pleural effusion showed evidence of transudate, and culture results for microorganisms tested were negative, including common aerobic and anaerobic bacterium as well as mycobacterium tuberculosis. Based on concerns about lead migration or protrusion-induced hemopericardium, the patient was subjected to chest computed tomography (CT), and no protrusion was detected (Fig. ). Additionally, the density of pericardial effusion was 20 Hounsfield unit (HU), which also did not support the possibility of hemopericardium. There was a limited improvement in the patient’s condition following several days of treatment, and echocardiography showed no worsening of pericardial effusion (thickness around 1.1 cm). Based on a suspicion of PCIS, the patient was prescribed prednisolone (30 mg/day initially), after which there was a dramatic improvement of his condition. The dosage of prednisolone was gradually tapered off to 20 mg/day after a week, 20 mg to 10 mg/day after two weeks, and the patient was maintained on 10 mg/day for 8 weeks. Although the CXR returned to baseline after completion of the steroid treatment (Fig. ), there was a recurrence of pleural effusion, leading to the resumption of low dose prednisolone treatment in addition to colchicine treatment. The patient recovered well after this treatment.
An 82-year-old male with a history of chronic atrial fibrillation (CHADS2: 3) was treated with rivaroxaban. The patient presented at the cardiology clinic with crescendo angina, and was reviewed with a coronary angiography examination, which showed significant focal stenosis at the orifice of the right coronary artery (RCA) (Fig. ). The patient was subjected to percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), where a Xience Xpedition stent (3.5/15 mm) was deployed at the orifice. The procedure was uneventful, and the final angiogram showed good RCA flow, and no evidence of perforation, dissection, or extravasations (Fig. ).
However, two hours after the procedure, the patient developed cold sweats, tightness in the chest, and hemodynamic compromise along with bradycardia (50 bpm) and hypotension (systolic blood pressure: 70–80 mm Hg). Although a complete electrocardiography (ECG) showed no abnormalities, echocardiography showed new pericardial effusion (thickness 1.1–1.5 cm) with RV early diastolic collapse. This was immediately followed by a repeat coronary angiography, which showed good RCA flow without any extravasation, perforation or thrombosis. A chest CT scan with contrast showed no aortic dissection, and the density of pericardial effusion suggested hemopericardium (HU: 40) (Fig. ). In addition to vasopressors which were administered to stabilize the hemodynamics, the patient was also prescribed a 50 mg dose of hydrocortisone for PCIS. There was an improvement in the patient’s condition on the second day and all vasopressors was discontinued in 18 h. The patient was discharged to the outpatient department with a prescription for 20 mg prednisolone, and remained stable at his follow-up visits. However, 9 months later, after we tapered off prednisolone, the patient had increased discomfort of dyspnea on exertion and the echocardiography showed pericardial effusion recurred. We prescribed colchicine and low dose prednisolone for its control and patient’s discomfort improved.

case_text:
A 64-year-old man with a 50 packs per year smoking history, COPD on three-liter (L) home oxygen, and right lung cancer status post resection 25 years prior to admission presented to the emergency room with worsening shortness of breath, non-productive cough, wheezing, and generalized weakness for the past few weeks. At presentation, vitals were notable for blood pressure of 165/98 mm Hg, tachypnea (RR 22/minute), and oxygen saturation of 92% on 3 L of nasal cannula. On physical examination, he was dyspneic, cachectic appearing with diminished breath sounds more on left hemithorax, and bilateral diffuse wheezing. Laboratory workup was unremarkable. Chest radiograph revealed bullous changes involving both upper lobes and particularly the left hemithorax. Mild blunting of the left costophrenic angle from a small left pleural effusion or pleural thickening was also seen (Figure ).
Given his respiratory distress and radiographic findings concerning for a pneumothorax, a CT of the chest was performed and pneumothorax was ruled out. On CT scan, we noted that giant bullae compressed the left lower lung lobe (Figures , ). These radiological findings were consistent with VLS that had initially mimicked a pneumothorax. Our patient was not deemed a candidate for lung volume reduction surgery. He improved modestly with oral prednisone and scheduled nebulizer treatments.

case_text:
A 17-year-old boy presented to the emergency room (ER) complaining of shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain that had developed 2 hours earlier. The patient was a high school student who had been well until 1 month before this visit. In the subsequent month, he had a dry cough, fatigue, and weight loss of 2 kg. He had no febrile sensation or myalgia. The day before, he developed fever, chills, and pleuritic chest pain rated 3 points on a 0-10 numeric pain intensity scale. The pain was located on the anterior chest wall and was aggravated when the patient inspired deeply. Two hours before visiting the ER, shortness of breath developed, and the pleuritic chest pain was aggravated and radiated to the shoulder and jaw. He did not smoke nor drink alcohol, and did not have any trauma.
The patient was alert but appeared acutely ill. Vital signs included a body temperature of 39.0℃, blood pressure of 107/70 mmHg, heart rate of 110 beats/min, respiratory rate of 30/min, and 98% oxygen saturation with pulse oximetry on room air. Results of examinations of the head, eye, ear, nose, and throat were unremarkable. The jugular vein was not distended. On chest examination, lung auscultation was normal, but a rapid and distant heart sound was heard. On abdominal examination, there was no tender point or organomegaly. No pitting edema on the peripheral limbs was observed.

case_text:
Case 2: A 74-year-old male with a 3-day history of fever, anorexia, vomiting, and shortness of breath was admitted to our hospital. The patient had no history of drug and alcohol abuse and was a non-smoker. His vital signs at admission were as follows: temperature of 38.2 °C, pulse rate of 110 beats per minute, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and SpO2 of 90% in ambient air. After a thorough workup including routine tests and computerized tomography, he received a treatment for COVID-19 and was discharged with good condition and reduced inflammatory markers. Twelve days later, he was readmitted with worsening dyspnea, palpitation, lethargy, confusion, drowsiness, blurring of vision, and generalized weakness. The initial vital signs included body temperature of 38 °C, pulse rate of 120 beats per minute, blood pressure of 140/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, and SpO2 of 85% while breathing ambient air. Cranial nerves examination was normal and his pupils were midsize and reactive to light and accommodation.
Laboratory data were as follows: blood glucose level, 102 mg/dL; BUN, 29.6 mg/dL; creatinine (Serum), 0.9 mg/dL; sodium, 138 mEq/L; potassium, 4.6mEq/L; magnesium: 1.7 mg/dL; phosphures, 4 mg/dL; calcium, 8.9mg/dL; ALP, 706 U/L; AST: 66 U/L, ALT: 53 U/L, and troponin level, 4 ng/mL. The blood sample revealed the following results: WBC count 10.4×109/L with 7% lymphocytes and 91% neutrophils; CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 128 mg/L and 57 mm/h, respectively. Chest CT scan showed bilateral GGOs which was expected due to the underlying COVID-19 infection (). The axial unenhanced CT image of the brain showed a hypodense lesion in the superior and lateral aspects of the left cerebellar hemisphere without significant mass effect (). Due to his atrial fibrillation (AF) pattern in the electrocardiogram (ECG), along with his fluctuating SpO2, the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Patient received heparin-based prophylaxis. A single 500 mg oral dose of chloroquine phosphate, Kaletra (lopinavir/ ritonavir) two 200 mg tablets twice daily, meropenem 1 g IV q8hr and vancomycin 1 gram q12hr were administered. After 3 days, his drowsiness diminished and he was able to tolerate oral diets. Also, his CRP level decreased to 63 mg/L. Therefore, he was transferred to the infectious diseases ward. Four days later, he developed arrhythmia, confusion and new-onset hemiplegia. At the time, WBC count was 10.00×109/L with 9.5% lymphocytes; pro BNP, 8930 pg/mL; D-dimer, 7500 μg/L; CRP, 203 mg/L and PCT, 0.2 ng/mL. Anticoagulant was started for him and he was readmitted to ICU. Nine days later, his condition improved and he was discharged with an SpO2 of 95% and CRP of 30 mg/L.

case_text:
12-year-old boy presented with history of trauma to his right ankle three days back. He complained of pain and swelling of right ankle. He also gave a history of associated cough and fever since 5 days. The personal and past history was insignificant.
Patient was febrile with 38.5 degree Celsius temperature; tachycardia at 125/min and respiratory rate 25/min. Right ankle was mildly swollen with redness, local rise of temperature, tenderness over lateral malleolus, lower 3rd leg laterally (). There was restriction of ankle movements. No neurovascular deficits. Rest of the limb was normal. Plain X-ray of right ankle with leg was normal. His blood parameters were; haemoglobin-12.5gm%;total count- 21.28K/uL; neutrophils-19.77K/uL; lymphocytes-0.75K/uL%, CRP- 360.1mg/L(positive); ESR--60mm/hr; RAfactor-negative; ASO-titre- 400IU/ML; sickling-negative. Urine routine was performed and found to benormal. Patient was admitted for treatment of suspected cellulitis, pediatric opinion was sought for cough. Chest X-ray: revealed pneumonia, therefore he was started on IV Cloxacillin 1gm four times daily. Later blood culture revealed growth of Staphylococcus aureus which was sensitive to Cloxaciilin. On the 3rd day, patient’s general condition deteriorated with persistently elevated temperature, tachycardia (140/min), respiratory rate at 40/min and SPO2- 87% at room air with moderate swelling on whole of right leg with tender calf and a positive Homan sign. D-Dimer test was negative. CT angiogram of chest was carried out to rule out pulmonary embolism. There was no evidence of embolism, but showed right sided pleural effusion and bilateral patchy pneumonia. The duplex scan of right lower limb was suggestive of popliteal vein thrombosis (, ), thrombophilia work up for protein C &S; anti- thrombin III was negative. Patient was treated with low molecular heparin and IV cloxacillin (for pneumonia) in intensive care unit. Patient improved clinically, calf swelling was reduced and blood parameters were also reverting to normalcy at the time of discharge. Patient was discharged on 14th day and was treated with warfarin for next 3 months. Repeat duplex scan at 6 weeks was normal. Patient was followed up for period of 6 months, and there were no signs of recurrence.

case_text:
A 62 year old female presented to the emergency room with history of fall from one storey building. The impact was over the trunk region. On clinical examination the blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, pulse rate was 110/min, temperature was 98.6 degree Farenheit and respiratory rate was 20/min. Pallor was present and the thyroid gland was enlarged. Pansystolic murmur was present over the mitral and tricuspid regions. Fine basal crepitations were heard over both lung fields. Left upper quadrant tenderness was present.
A complete blood count showed pancytopenia with hemoglobin 7.4gm/dl (normal: 12–16 gm/dl), WBC count 3400/μl (normal: 4000–11,000/μl) and platelet count 91,000/μl (normal 1,50,000-4,00,000/μl). Multiple ventricular premature complexes were present in the electrocardiogram (ECG). Ultrasound of the abdomen showed splenic laceration with splenic hematoma extending up to the hilum. Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed findings consistent with grade II splenic injury.
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for conservative management and further workup with the impression of grade II splenic injury and pancytopenia.
Ultrasound of the neck showed multiple heteroechoic nodules with calcification in both lobes of thyroid, findings suggestive of multinodular goiter. Echocardiography showed severe tricuspid regurgitation and mitral regurgitation. Bone marrow aspiration showed mixed normocellular and a few hypercellular marrow fragments. Absolute retics and peripheral blood smear were normal. Hormonal studies showed features suggestive of hyperthyroidism (Table ).
The patients hemoglobin improved with two units of packed cells transfusion but the WBC and platelet count didn’t improve. On the third day of admission, she developed a temperature of 102 degree Farenheit, pulse rate of 150-160/min, respiratory rate of 30/min and oxygen saturation of 75-80% at 5 L/min of oxygen via face mask. On examination the patient was agitated and had diffuse crepitations over both lung fields. On ECG monitoring multiple VPCs per minute was present. A Burch Wartofsky Score of 95 was calculated (Table ). With the impression of thyroid storm, the patient was started on hydrocortisone, oral propranolol 40 mg q6hrly (intravenous preparation not available), and oral carbimazole 10 mg q8hrly. After 24 hours the patients pulse rate stabilized between 80–100 bpm, temperature was 99 degree farenheit and there were only few VPCs per minute. Propranolol was gradually tapered over a period of one week and her pulse rate stabilized at 60 to 80 bpm. After starting carbimazole, her WBC and platelet counts started improving and became normal at discharge (Table ).
The patient was advised for radionuclide thyroid scan and further treatment.

1. Temperature >38°C (100.4°F) or <36°C (96.8°F): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
2. Heart rate >90: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
3. Respiratory rate >20 or PaCO₂ <32 mm Hg: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point

case_text:
A 62 year old female presented to the emergency room with history of fall from one storey building. The impact was over the trunk region. On clinical examination the blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, pulse rate was 110/min, temperature was 98.6 degree Farenheit and respiratory rate was 20/min. Pallor was present and the thyroid gland was enlarged. Pansystolic murmur was present over the mitral and tricuspid regions. Fine basal crepitations were heard over both lung fields. Left upper quadrant tenderness was present.
A complete blood count showed pancytopenia with hemoglobin 7.4gm/dl (normal: 12–16 gm/dl), WBC count 3400/μl (normal: 4000–11,000/μl) and platelet count 91,000/μl (normal 1,50,000-4,00,000/μl). Multiple ventricular premature complexes were present in the electrocardiogram (ECG). Ultrasound of the abdomen showed splenic laceration with splenic hematoma extending up to the hilum. Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed findings consistent with grade II splenic injury.
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for conservative management and further workup with the impression of grade II splenic injury and pancytopenia.
Ultrasound of the neck showed multiple heteroechoic nodules with calcification in both lobes of thyroid, findings suggestive of multinodular goiter. Echocardiography showed severe tricuspid regurgitation and mitral regurgitation. Bone marrow aspiration showed mixed normocellular and a few hypercellular marrow fragments. Absolute retics and peripheral blood smear were normal. Hormonal studies showed features suggestive of hyperthyroidism (Table ).
The patients hemoglobin improved with two units of packed cells transfusion but the WBC and platelet count didn’t improve. On the third day of admission, she developed a temperature of 102 degree Farenheit, pulse rate of 150-160/min, respiratory rate of 25/min and oxygen saturation of 75-80% at 5 L/min of oxygen via face mask. On examination the patient was agitated and had diffuse crepitations over both lung fields. On ECG monitoring multiple VPCs per minute was present. A Burch Wartofsky Score of 95 was calculated (Table ). With the impression of thyroid storm, the patient was started on hydrocortisone, oral propranolol 40 mg q6hrly (intravenous preparation not available), and oral carbimazole 10 mg q8hrly. After 24 hours the patients pulse rate stabilized between 80–100 bpm, temperature was 99 degree farenheit and there were only few VPCs per minute. Propranolol was gradually tapered over a period of one week and her pulse rate stabilized at 60 to 80 bpm. After starting carbimazole, her WBC and platelet counts started improving and became normal at discharge (Table ).
The patient was advised for radionuclide thyroid scan and further treatment.

case_text: A 62-year-old man with a background of insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with a long-acting bronchodilator, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and remote alcohol use disorder was transported to our emergency department from a skilled-nursing facility after staff noted a sudden decline in responsiveness accompanied by labored breathing and a recorded fever of 38.9 °C; he had completed a five-day course of oral levofloxacin for presumed bronchitis one week earlier but never fully returned to baseline energy. According to the transfer paperwork, he ambulated with a walker the day before but spoke in single words and appeared confused on the morning of presentation. Paramedics found him slumped over the side rails of his bed, moaning but without purposeful movement, saturating 82 % on room air. They applied a high-concentration Venturi mask set to deliver 55 % inspired oxygen and transported him in a semi-upright position; no sedation, paralytic agents, or advanced airway devices were used en route, and there were no intravenous fluids started in the field. Ten minutes after arrival in our resuscitation bay—before any antibiotic, crystalloid bolus, or vasoactive infusion had been administered—his vital signs revealed a heart rate of 124 beats per minute in sinus tachycardia, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, temperature 39.2 °C, and a cuff blood pressure repeatedly measured at 84/44 mm Hg with a mean in the mid-50s. Peripheral pulses were faint, capillary refill exceeded four seconds, and the skin of the distal extremities was mottled and cool to touch. An arterial blood sample drawn from the right radial artery while he remained on 55 % FiO₂ yielded a PaO₂ of 88 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 42 mm Hg, pH 7.31, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. On neurologic examination he did not open his eyes to voice or to nail-bed pressure, emitted only guttural incomprehensible sounds, and demonstrated bilateral extension at the elbows with internal rotation of the shoulders when the sternum was rubbed, for a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 5; pupils were 4 mm and sluggish but symmetric, corneal reflexes were present, and there was no lateralizing deficit. Auscultation of the chest disclosed coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower two thirds and scattered wheezes bilaterally, while percussion was dull over the same right basilar segment. Cardiac examination showed a rapid regular rhythm without murmurs, jugular venous pressure was not appreciable in the sitting position, and the abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding. A bedside bladder scan after Foley insertion registered minimal volume, and the initial catheter drainage produced only 30 mL of dark amber urine; review of the facility flow sheet handed to the triage nurse documented an aggregate urinary output of 700 mL during the preceding twenty-four hours. Initial laboratory studies obtained from the first venipuncture demonstrated a white blood cell count of 21.3 × 10³/µL with 15 % bands, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 37 %, and a platelet count of 110 000/µL. Serum chemistry panel returned sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, glucose 198 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, and a creatinine of 2.2 mg/dL, representing a clear rise from his documented baseline of 1.5 mg/dL two months earlier. Hepatic indices revealed total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 44 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L; coagulation profile showed an international normalized ratio of 1.6 and activated partial thromboplastin time 45 seconds. High-sensitivity troponin I was 0.05 ng/mL, and procalcitonin measured 38 ng/mL. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph taken within fifteen minutes of arrival demonstrated a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small adjacent pleural effusion but no obvious cardiomegaly. Computed tomography of the head without contrast, performed promptly because of the depressed sensorium, revealed only chronic microvascular changes without hemorrhage or mass effect. The patient’s medication list included metformin (held at the facility because of poor oral intake), glargine insulin, tiotropium inhaler, and low-dose aspirin; he was not receiving corticosteroids or anticoagulation, and nursing notes denied recent nephrotoxic exposures. He consumed alcohol socially in the distant past, had quit smoking ten years ago after a twenty-pack-year history, and had no known drug allergies. The working impression on arrival favored severe community-acquired pneumonia with systemic inflammatory response, progressing to distributive shock, acute encephalopathy, evolving acute kidney injury on chronic disease, and early consumptive thrombocytopenia. Airway protection, aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and possible vasopressor support were all discussed with the attending physician, but at the moment the data above were captured the patient remained breathing spontaneously through the 55 % oxygen mask, still profoundly obtunded and hypotensive, without having yet received any therapeutic intervention in our emergency department.

case_text: A 45-year-old woman with morbid obesity, insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes, recurrent urinary-tract infections related to neurogenic bladder from childhood spina bifida, and untreated obstructive sleep apnea was discovered at 04:30 by her partner lying on the bedroom floor, intermittently moaning and incontinent of urine after reporting fever and flank discomfort the previous evening; emergency medical services arrived ten minutes later to find her febrile at 38.9 °C, tachypneic to the high thirties, and obtunded with gurgling respirations and peripheral oxygen saturation in the mid-70 % range on room air. Because she had copious gastric contents and could not protect her airway, the paramedic crew performed rapid-sequence intubation with etomidate and succinylcholine, placed a 7.5-mm cuffed endotracheal tube on first attempt, and transferred her to a transport ventilator in volume assist-control mode: tidal volume 500 mL, respiratory rate 20, 5 cm H₂O of positive end-expiratory pressure, and an inspired-oxygen fraction documented at 0.55; no bag-mask ventilation or non-invasive positive-pressure interface had been attempted beforehand, and she received neither crystalloid bolus, vasoactive medication, nor antimicrobial therapy during the nine-minute transport. On arrival to the emergency department resuscitation bay—before any hospital interventions were started—she remained connected to the same ventilator settings with synchronised chest excursions and peak airway pressure of 24 cm H₂O. An arterial line was inserted in the left radial artery within three minutes, and the first blood gas obtained while she was still on 55 % inspired oxygen revealed pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, and PaO₂ 62 mm Hg. Simultaneous automated blood-pressure cuff reading, confirmed by arterial waveform, showed 91/54 mm Hg with a mean of 66 mm Hg; heart rate was 128 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate matched the set 20 breaths per minute, and tympanic temperature measured 39.1 °C. Capillary refill was four seconds, extremities were cool, and jugular veins were flat at 30°. After a short pause in sedatives the neurologic examination demonstrated that she opened her eyes to loud voice, uttered confused phrases around the deflated cuff, and withdrew purposefully to nail-bed pressure in all four extremities, giving a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 11 without focal asymmetry; pupils were 3 mm and briskly reactive, corneal and cough reflexes were present, and there was no nuchal rigidity. Breath sounds were decreased at the bases with scattered coarse crackles but symmetric, and the endotracheal tube was 3 cm above the carina on bedside ultrasound. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was distended, tender in the right costovertebral angle, and tympanitic without rebound or guarding; a firm bladder was palpable midway to the umbilicus. Skin inspection showed mild scleral icterus and scattered livedoid patches over the shins but no purpura or petechiae. A 16-French Foley catheter placed during the primary survey immediately drained 60 mL of cloudy amber urine with foul odor; the partner, who routinely measures outputs because of the patient’s intermittent self-catheterization, reported an estimated total of 920 mL voided over the previous twenty-four hours. Laboratory studies drawn concurrently with the arterial sample—before any intravenous fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors, or renal-support measures were begun—demonstrated sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, glucose 236 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.25 mg/dL, slightly above her documented baseline of 0.9 mg/dL from a nephrology visit one month earlier. The complete blood count returned white-blood-cell count 22.4 × 10³/µL with 18 % band forms, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, hematocrit 35 %, and platelet count 123 000 /µL. Hepatic panel showed aspartate aminotransferase 69 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L, total bilirubin 1.55 mg/dL with predominantly direct fraction, and an international normalized ratio of 1.3. Venous lactate was 4.2 mmol/L. Point-of-care ultrasound revealed moderate right hydronephrosis with echogenic debris in the collecting system, a non-dilated inferior vena cava that collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, and a hyperdynamic left ventricle without pericardial effusion. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained while the patient remained on the transport ventilator demonstrated diffuse atelectasis but clear lung fields and correct tube placement. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded sinus tachycardia at 126 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T changes, no ischemic pattern, and a corrected QT interval of 432 ms. At the exact moment these physiologic measurements and laboratory values were captured, she had not yet received crystalloid resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressor infusion, insulin, or renal decompressive procedures; she continued to breathe through the endotracheal tube on a volume-controlled ventilator delivering 0.55 inspired oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 62 mm Hg, perfused tenuously at 91/54 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, exhibited moderate thrombocytopenia, mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, early renal impairment with reduced urine output, and remained encephalopathic but responsive to painful stimulus in the setting of presumed obstructive urosepsis.

case_text: A 45-year-old woman with morbid obesity, insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes, recurrent urinary-tract infections related to neurogenic bladder from childhood spina bifida, and untreated obstructive sleep apnea was discovered at 04:30 by her partner lying on the bedroom floor, intermittently moaning and incontinent of urine after reporting fever and flank discomfort the previous evening; emergency medical services arrived ten minutes later to find her febrile at 38.9 °C, tachypneic to the high thirties, and obtunded with gurgling respirations and peripheral oxygen saturation in the mid-70 % range on room air. Because she had copious gastric contents and could not protect her airway, the paramedic crew performed rapid-sequence intubation with etomidate and succinylcholine, placed a 7.5-mm cuffed endotracheal tube on first attempt, and transferred her to a transport ventilator in volume assist-control mode: tidal volume 500 mL, respiratory rate 20, 5 cm H₂O of positive end-expiratory pressure, and an inspired-oxygen fraction documented at 0.55; no bag-mask ventilation or non-invasive positive-pressure interface had been attempted beforehand, and she received neither crystalloid bolus, vasoactive medication, nor antimicrobial therapy during the nine-minute transport. On arrival to the emergency department resuscitation bay—before any hospital interventions were started—she remained connected to the same ventilator settings with synchronised chest excursions and peak airway pressure of 24 cm H₂O. An arterial line was inserted in the left radial artery within three minutes, and the first blood gas obtained while she was still on 55 % inspired oxygen revealed pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, and PaO₂ 62 mm Hg. Simultaneous automated blood-pressure cuff reading, confirmed by arterial waveform, showed 91/54 mm Hg with a mean of 66 mm Hg; heart rate was 128 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate matched the set 20 breaths per minute, and tympanic temperature measured 39.1 °C. Capillary refill was four seconds, extremities were cool, and jugular veins were flat at 30°. After a short pause in sedatives the neurologic examination demonstrated that she opened her eyes to loud voice, uttered confused phrases around the deflated cuff, and withdrew purposefully to nail-bed pressure in all four extremities, giving a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 11 without focal asymmetry; pupils were 3 mm and briskly reactive, corneal and cough reflexes were present, and there was no nuchal rigidity. Breath sounds were decreased at the bases with scattered coarse crackles but symmetric, and the endotracheal tube was 3 cm above the carina on bedside ultrasound. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was distended, tender in the right costovertebral angle, and tympanitic without rebound or guarding; a firm bladder was palpable midway to the umbilicus. Skin inspection showed mild scleral icterus and scattered livedoid patches over the shins but no purpura or petechiae. A 16-French Foley catheter placed during the primary survey immediately drained 60 mL of cloudy amber urine with foul odor; the partner, who routinely measures outputs because of the patient’s intermittent self-catheterization, reported an estimated total of 474 mL voided over the previous twenty-four hours. Laboratory studies drawn concurrently with the arterial sample—before any intravenous fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors, or renal-support measures were begun—demonstrated sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, glucose 236 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.25 mg/dL, slightly above her documented baseline of 0.9 mg/dL from a nephrology visit one month earlier. The complete blood count returned white-blood-cell count 22.4 × 10³/µL with 18 % band forms, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, hematocrit 35 %, and platelet count 123 000 /µL. Hepatic panel showed aspartate aminotransferase 69 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L, total bilirubin 1.55 mg/dL with predominantly direct fraction, and an international normalized ratio of 1.3. Venous lactate was 4.2 mmol/L. Point-of-care ultrasound revealed moderate right hydronephrosis with echogenic debris in the collecting system, a non-dilated inferior vena cava that collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, and a hyperdynamic left ventricle without pericardial effusion. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained while the patient remained on the transport ventilator demonstrated diffuse atelectasis but clear lung fields and correct tube placement. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded sinus tachycardia at 126 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T changes, no ischemic pattern, and a corrected QT interval of 432 ms. At the exact moment these physiologic measurements and laboratory values were captured, she had not yet received crystalloid resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressor infusion, insulin, or renal decompressive procedures; she continued to breathe through the endotracheal tube on a volume-controlled ventilator delivering 0.55 inspired oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 62 mm Hg, perfused tenuously at 91/54 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, exhibited moderate thrombocytopenia, mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, early renal impairment with reduced urine output, and remained encephalopathic but responsive to painful stimulus in the setting of presumed obstructive urosepsis.

case_text: A 48-year-old woman with a history of morbid obesity complicated by untreated type 2 diabetes, mild alcoholic steatohepatitis, and nightly home use of a bedside flow generator for obstructive sleep apnoea was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after two days of rigors, pleuritic right-sided chest discomfort, and progressively laboured breathing that culminated in a syncopal episode while walking from the bedroom to the bathroom thirty minutes before arrival; she had taken no prescription medications for the past year except over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain and denied recent antibiotic exposure, diuretic use, or corticosteroid therapy. Paramedics found her seated on the bedroom floor, speaking in short phrases between gasps, diaphoretic, and noticeably drowsy but arousable; oxygen saturation on room air measured 83 % and systolic pressure on the thigh cuff was in the mid-90s. They fitted her own full-face sleep mask to the transport circuit, dialled the machine to deliver approximately 10 cm H₂O of continuous distending pressure augmented by wall oxygen that their inline analyser recorded at 0.39 fraction of inspired oxygen, and established a single 18-gauge antecubital line without giving any crystalloids, vasopressors, or analgesics during the nine-minute transport. On stretcher entry to the resuscitation bay—still prior to any hospital therapy—she remained on the same pressure-supported circuit, generating each breath herself, coughing intermittently but denying chest pain. Initial vitals captured within the first minute showed temperature 38.2 °C tympanic, heart rate 118 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute with accessory muscle usage, and non-invasive blood pressure 96/57 mm Hg confirmed moments later by a right radial arterial line. Extremities were cool with capillary refill of three seconds, jugular veins were flat at 30°, and there was faint peripheral mottling over the knees. Neurologic assessment undertaken before any sedative or opiate administration revealed pupils 3 mm and briskly reactive, spontaneous eye opening, confused speech occasionally mixing dates and places, and purposeful localisation of trapezius squeeze with both arms, yielding a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 12; no focal weakness, pronator drift, or asterixis was observed. Pulmonary examination demonstrated inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right middle and lower lung zones, diminished air movement on the left base, and equal chest rise around the harnessed face mask; there was no tracheal deviation or wheeze. Cardiac auscultation noted a tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was soft, mildly distended, nontender, and the liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the costal margin with no palpable spleen. Skin survey revealed scattered spider angiomata on the anterior chest and faint icterus of the sclerae but no petechiae or ecchymoses. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted immediately after arterial cannulation drained 85 mL of concentrated amber urine; her spouse, who tracks her fluid intake because of prior nephrology visits, estimated total voided volume of roughly 980 mL over the last twenty-four hours. Within five minutes, while she remained on the 0.39 inspired fraction delivered through the continuous distending interface, a radial arterial blood gas returned pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 42 mm Hg, bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L, and PaO₂ 96 mm Hg. Concurrent laboratory studies drawn from the arterial line—before any crystalloid bolus, antimicrobial, antipyretic, or vasoactive infusion—revealed sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, glucose 186 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.38 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL measured at an outpatient clinic eight months earlier. Total bilirubin returned at 1.35 mg/dL with predominantly conjugated fraction; aspartate aminotransferase was 72 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 180 U/L, and international normalised ratio 1.2. The complete blood count showed leukocytes 15.1 ×10³/µL with 12 % band forms, haemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, haematocrit 39 %, and a platelet concentration of 152 000 /µL. High-sensitivity troponin was undetectable, pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was 218 pg/mL, and C-reactive protein measured 142 mg/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained while she remained seated upright in the resuscitation bay illustrated a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, mild cardiomegaly, and no pleural effusion or pneumothorax; the face mask straps and arterial catheter were appropriately positioned. Bedside focused cardiac ultrasound demonstrated a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle, no pericardial effusion, and an inferior vena cava collapsing more than 50 % with inspiration. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram confirmed sinus tachycardia at 120 beats per minute without ischaemic ST-segment changes and a corrected QT interval of 408 ms. At the instant all of the above physiologic and biochemical data were captured, the patient remained awake, breathing spontaneously through the constant distending-pressure system supplying 0.39 FiO₂, perfusing marginally at 96/57 mm Hg without any catecholamine support, exhibiting moderate encephalopathy, mild thrombocytopenia, subtly elevated bilirubin, early renal impairment with borderline daily oliguria, and an arterial oxygen tension of 96 mm Hg—all recorded prior to initiation of intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, or further respiratory support.

case_text: A 55-year-old man with longstanding non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (latest outpatient echocardiogram two weeks earlier showed an ejection fraction of 20 %), insulin-treated diabetes, and chronic tobacco and alcohol use was brought directly from his apartment by advanced life support after his visiting nurse found him gasping for air, clammy, and confused while still connected to his portable inotrope pump that administers dobutamine 5 mcg/kg/min through a right basilic PICC line. According to emergency personnel, he was sitting upright in bed, speaking only single words, and peripheral pulse oximetry registered 78 % on room air. Rapid-sequence intubation with etomidate and rocuronium was performed on scene; a 7.5-mm cuffed endotracheal tube was secured at 22 cm at the incisors, and he was transferred onto a transport ventilator set to volume assist-control, tidal volume 480 mL, rate 22 breaths per minute, 6 cm H₂O of positive end-expiratory pressure, and an inspired oxygen fraction of 0.56, parameters left unchanged during the ten-minute ride. No crystalloid bolus, antibiotics, vasopressors beyond the home infusion, steroids, diuretics, or sedative infusion were initiated by the crew. On entry to the resuscitation bay—and before any additional hospital interventions—a right radial arterial catheter was placed, yielding an immediate gas that demonstrated pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, bicarbonate 17 mEq/L, and a PaO₂ of 79 mm Hg on the documented 56 % FiO₂. Simultaneous non-invasive blood pressure cycled twice at 88/49 mm Hg with a thread of a radial pulse of 112 beats per minute, skin mottled to both knees, and neck veins mildly distended. Despite being intubated, he opened his eyes to voice, mumbled his name and the month but could not state the year, and localized pain in all extremities, producing a Glasgow Coma Score of 13; pupils were symmetric at 3 mm and briskly reactive, corneal and cough reflexes were intact, and no lateralizing deficits were evident. Auscultation revealed diffuse coarse crackles more prominent over the right mid-lung field and scattered rhonchi; heart sounds were rapid but regular without new murmurs or gallops. The distal abdomen was soft, nontender, and without organomegaly, though the mid-epigastrium displayed a healing laparoscopic scar from a feeding-tube removal performed months earlier. Extremities were cool with sluggish capillary refill, and the PICC site was clean and intact. A 16-F Foley catheter inserted as part of primary survey immediately drained 45 mL of concentrated tea-colored urine; review of the visiting nurse’s electronic flow sheet, which logs all voids because of the patient’s diuretic titrations, indicated an aggregate 900 mL of urine over the preceding twenty-four hours. Blood drawn from the arterial line and peripheral venipuncture, all resulted before any emergency department-initiated medication or fluid, showed white blood cell count 15.8 × 10³/µL with 12 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, and a platelet count of 127 000 /µL. Comprehensive metabolic profile returned sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, anion gap 18, glucose 168 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL compared with a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL noted in clinic a month prior. Total bilirubin measured 1.4 mg/dL with predominantly direct fraction; aspartate aminotransferase 62 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 186 U/L, and international normalized ratio 1.4. High-sensitivity troponin was negative, lactate 4.7 mmol/L, pro-B-type natriuretic peptide exceeded assay upper limit, and C-reactive protein was markedly elevated. Bedside lung ultrasound performed within five minutes showed subpleural consolidations with static air bronchograms in the right lower lobe and diffuse B-lines bilaterally, whereas focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a severely dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis, trivial pericardial effusion, and a collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.2 cm. Portable chest radiograph obtained while he remained on the transport ventilator depicted patchy right lower-zone opacities, an endotracheal tip 3 cm above the carina, and enlarged cardiac silhouette without pleural free air. Electrocardiogram recorded concurrently displayed sinus tachycardia at 110 beats per minute with left bundle-branch block unchanged from prior. Up to this moment, the patient continued to receive only his chronic inotrope at 5 mcg/kg/min, remained hypotensive with systolic pressure in the high 80s, was mechanically ventilated on 56 % oxygen yielding the arterial oxygen tension of 79 mm Hg, demonstrated mild thrombocytopenia, modest hyperbilirubinemia, acute kidney injury with oliguria, and an altered level of consciousness attributable to systemic hypoperfusion and evolving sepsis likely secondary to multifocal pneumonia.

case_text: A 49-year-old woman with a background of insulin-requiring diabetes, stage-2 chronic kidney disease noted on primary-care labs six months earlier (baseline creatinine 1.2 mg/dL), and longstanding obstructive sleep apnea for which she owns a home bilevel device was discovered at 05:40 slumped against the hallway wall by her teenage son after two days of febrile chills, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and progressively labored breathing that kept her from lying flat overnight. Emergency medical technicians arrived within seven minutes to find her sitting forward on the floor, clutching her chest, drenched in sweat, and speaking in two-word gasps while an inexpensive finger oximeter flashed 72 % on ambient air. Because she repeatedly retched when a basic airway adjunct was attempted yet still maintained cough and gag, the crew elected not to place an endotracheal tube; instead they fitted a tight oronasal interface connected to their portable turbine delivering a continuous distending pressure of 12 cm H₂O and blended oxygen the inline analyzer documented at 0.67. Despite that support her saturation never climbed above the high 70s, and an automated cuff on the right arm cycled twice at 82/48 and 88/52 mm Hg, prompting early notification to the receiving hospital but no vasopressors or crystalloid during the eight-minute transport. On arrival in the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital-initiated medication, intravenous fluid, or adjustment of the noninvasive settings—she remained propped upright against the CPAP cushion, respirations shallow at 30/min with pronounced sternocleidomastoid recruitment, skin cool and pale with beads of sweat over the upper lip, and capillary refill roughly four seconds. A left radial arterial catheter was sited on first attempt; the initial gas obtained three minutes after stretcher touchdown showed pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 45 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, and a striking PaO₂ of 56 mm Hg while the delivered inspired fraction remained 67 %. Concurrent noninvasive blood pressure confirmed 86/50 mm Hg with a feeble radial pulse of 118 beats per minute in sinus rhythm. Neurologic appraisal revealed eyes opening to voice, slurred but comprehensible answers that failed to provide the correct date, and brisk withdrawal to supra-orbital notch pressure, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13; pupils were equal at 3 mm and reactive, corneal and gag reflexes were intact, and there was no focal asymmetry of power or tone. Chest examination demonstrated asymmetric excursion with reduced expansion over the right posterior lung field, diffuse coarse crackles more prominent at the base, and occasional bronchial breaths; percussion in that region was dull, and whispered pectoriloquy was present. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, jugular veins were flat at 30°, and no peripheral edema was appreciated. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant but without rebound or guarding; bowel sounds were present. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the primary survey drained 40 mL of concentrated amber urine, and the son’s smartphone hydration app—into which she logs voids for nephrology follow-up—showed cumulative urinary output of 960 mL over the last twenty-four hours. Laboratory specimens drawn simultaneously with the arterial sample and resulted before any antibiotic, vasopressor, or fluid reached the patient revealed white blood cell count 18.2 × 10³/µL with 15 % band forms, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 36 %, and a platelet concentration of 101 000 /µL. Serum chemistry demonstrated sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, glucose 186 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. Hepatic indices showed aspartate aminotransferase 42 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 48 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 158 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.2. High-sensitivity troponin was 0.05 ng/mL, procalcitonin measured 11 ng/mL, and venous lactate matched the arterial at 4.3 mmol/L. A bedside lung ultrasound performed within five minutes depicted shred sign and dynamic air bronchograms in the right lower lobe with scattered B-lines elsewhere, while focused cardiac sonography revealed a small hyperdynamic left ventricle and a collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.1 cm. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained without interrupting the CPAP circuit demonstrated a dense right lower-zone consolidation, patchy infiltrates in the middle lobe, and no pneumothorax. Twelve-lead electrocardiography recorded sinus tachycardia at 118 beats/min with nonspecific ST-T changes and a corrected QT interval of 460 ms. Up to the exact moment these physiologic and biochemical data were captured, she had received neither crystalloid nor vasoactive medication, remained on face-mask continuous positive airway pressure delivering 67 % oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 56 mm Hg, continued to exhibit a systolic pressure no higher than 86 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, displayed moderate thrombocytopenia, preserved bilirubin, an elevated creatinine alongside sub-one-liter urine output for the day, and evidenced only mild encephalopathy while teetering on the verge of overt septic shock likely from multilobar community-acquired pneumonia.
