case_text: A 26-year-old woman who works as an elementary-school art teacher and shares a basement apartment with two roommates presented to the emergency department in the early afternoon after waking with a second night of shaking chills, pleuritic left-sided chest discomfort, and an incessant dry cough that turned scantily productive only this morning; she measured an oral temperature of 38 °C at home, declined the acetaminophen her roommate offered, and rode a rideshare the ten city blocks to the hospital so the clinical team could record an unaltered physiologic profile. Her medical history is notable for stage IIB Hodgkin lymphoma treated with ABVD chemotherapy four years ago, followed by a consolidative involved-field radiation course; she has remained in complete remission on annual surveillance, takes no chronic medications beyond a daily vitamin, and has no record of kidney impairment, cerebrovascular insult, chronic liver disorder, or cardiomyopathy. She never smoked, drinks a single cider on rare weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Immunization records in the state registry confirm receipt of both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s inactivated influenza vaccine. On arrival she sat bolt upright on the stretcher, conversing in full sentences, maintaining eye contact, and correctly stating the date, location, and current national holiday, without agitation or confusion. Untreated triage vital signs while breathing ambient air at this sea-level facility measured: oral temperature 38.05 °C, an impressively rapid and regular radial pulse of 147 beats per minute corroborated on a three-lead monitor as sinus tachycardia without ectopy, automated blood pressure 123/71 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted for a full minute at 62 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and visible alar flaring, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 96 % and 97 %. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic but capillary refill remained brisk; conjunctivae appeared ruddy, and there was no digital clubbing or peripheral edema. Jugular venous pulsation did not rise above the sternal angle at 45°, and heart sounds revealed a forceful S1/S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Pulmonary examination disclosed coarse crackles over the left mid-axillary and posterior lower fields with preserved resonance to percussion; the right lung transmitted vesicular breath sounds throughout, and no dull stony note suggesting free fluid was elicited in either costophrenic recess. The abdomen was flat and nontender with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. A focused neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, 5/5 symmetric strength, and a normal finger-to-nose test. Capillary glucose obtained before vascular access read 158 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of bay entry—prior to any crystalloid bolus, antibiotics, or heparinized saline larger than the 3 mL used to lock the catheter—revealed sodium 108 mEq/L, potassium 3.7 mEq/L, chloride 79 mEq/L, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 13.4 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit a striking 67 %, hemoglobin 22.1 g/dL, and platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L. A right radial arterial sample obtained as she remained on room air showed pH 7.74, PaCO₂ 19 mm Hg, PaO₂ 108 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis driven by her profound tachypnea. Serum lactate measured 1.9 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin fell below the assay threshold. Portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs acquired fifteen minutes into the encounter—well before any antimicrobials, corticosteroids, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen—demonstrated a patchy consolidation in the lingular segment of the left upper lobe extending toward the inferior hilum without costophrenic angle blunting, layering opacity, or meniscus sign, and with a cardiac silhouette of normal size. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 146 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes but no acute ischemic pattern. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, a nurse-assisted expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any empiric therapy was initiated. Up to the moment this narrative is filed she has received no intravenous fluids, antipyretics, vasopressors, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or supplemental oxygen, ensuring that every vital sign, laboratory value, and imaging finding above reflects her untreated presentation.

case_text:
A 64-year-old male patient was referred to the emergency department of our hospital, with a four-day history of spontaneous abdominal pain radiating on the posterior aspect of the left thigh. He reported no trauma history, but during the past few hours, pain had severely deteriorated. In regards to his past medical history, the patient was on treatment for hypertension and atrial fibrillation. In particular, he was on an angiotensin II receptor blocker and on warfarin as an oral anticoagulant.
The patient was afebrile, and his vital signs were within normal values (blood pressure 115/78 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min, SpO2 99%). Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal pain, radiating on the posterior aspect of the left thigh. Peripheral vascular examination was within normal values on both lower limbs, with palpable pulses and capillary refill time of less than two seconds. Neurological condition, on the other hand, was impaired on the left lower limb, and objective deficiencies were obvious. Examination revealed reduced strength of the left lower limb. The patient was unable to straight leg raise, to flex the hip or the knee, and had developed hypoesthesia on the anterior aspect of the thigh. The patella reflex was absent on the affected side.
Laboratory data revealed prolonged prothrombin time with an international normalized ratio (INR) level of 4.5, and a haematocrit and haemoglobin decrease of 33.1% and 10.7 g/l, respectively. The rest of the full laboratory analysis was within normal values. Imaging studies included abdominal ultrasound scan (US), lumbar spine, and pelvis CT scans. Lumbar spine pathology was excluded, and a large retroperitoneal haematoma was unveiled within and around the left iliopsoas muscle (35 cm x 9 cm x 6 cm) (Figure ).
The patient was admitted to the hospital, and warfarin anticoagulation regimen was intermitted. Prolonged INR was reversed within 48 hours with the aid of vitamin K administration. A new CT scan was performed on day 3 post-admission. No change in the size of the haematoma was revealed (Figure ). At that point, there was a consultation with the radiology department whether the haematoma could be percutaneously drained; however, the CT scan revealed a clotted formation that would not allow for successful drainage.
The patient was managed conservatively. Physical therapy had been initiated by day 1 post-admission. The patient was discharged after six days of hospitalization and after pain management had been established. Nerve conduction studies were performed three weeks later and revealed left femoral nerve palsy. A new CT scan was performed two months post-discharge and unveiled absorption and a significantly reduced size of the haematoma (Figure ). The patient demonstrated gradual improvement and recovered after eight months of physiotherapy and rehabilitation. This included almost complete motor and complete sensory function restoration of the left femoral nerve.

case_text:
A 64-year-old male patient was referred to the emergency department of our hospital, with a four-day history of spontaneous abdominal pain radiating on the posterior aspect of the left thigh. The patient's sister has peripheral artery disease. He reported no trauma history, but during the past few hours, pain had severely deteriorated. In regards to his past medical history, the patient was on treatment for hypertension and atrial fibrillation. In particular, he was on an angiotensin II receptor blocker and on warfarin as an oral anticoagulant.
The patient was afebrile, and his vital signs were within normal values (blood pressure 115/78 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min, SpO2 99%). Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal pain, radiating on the posterior aspect of the left thigh. Peripheral vascular examination was within normal values on both lower limbs, with palpable pulses and capillary refill time of less than two seconds. Neurological condition, on the other hand, was impaired on the left lower limb, and objective deficiencies were obvious. Examination revealed reduced strength of the left lower limb. The patient was unable to straight leg raise, to flex the hip or the knee, and had developed hypoesthesia on the anterior aspect of the thigh. The patella reflex was absent on the affected side.
Laboratory data revealed prolonged prothrombin time with an international normalized ratio (INR) level of 4.5, and a haematocrit and haemoglobin decrease of 33.1% and 10.7 g/l, respectively. The rest of the full laboratory analysis was within normal values. Imaging studies included abdominal ultrasound scan (US), lumbar spine, and pelvis CT scans. Lumbar spine pathology was excluded, and a large retroperitoneal haematoma was unveiled within and around the left iliopsoas muscle (35 cm x 9 cm x 6 cm) (Figure ).
The patient was admitted to the hospital, and warfarin anticoagulation regimen was intermitted. Prolonged INR was reversed within 48 hours with the aid of vitamin K administration. A new CT scan was performed on day 3 post-admission. No change in the size of the haematoma was revealed (Figure ). At that point, there was a consultation with the radiology department whether the haematoma could be percutaneously drained; however, the CT scan revealed a clotted formation that would not allow for successful drainage.
The patient was managed conservatively. Physical therapy had been initiated by day 1 post-admission. The patient was discharged after six days of hospitalization and after pain management had been established. Nerve conduction studies were performed three weeks later and revealed left femoral nerve palsy. A new CT scan was performed two months post-discharge and unveiled absorption and a significantly reduced size of the haematoma (Figure ). The patient demonstrated gradual improvement and recovered after eight months of physiotherapy and rehabilitation. This included almost complete motor and complete sensory function restoration of the left femoral nerve.

case_text:
A 63-year-old man presented to the Accident and Emergency department with a history of mild frontal headache and progressive right-sided weakness. He was on bendrofluazide and atenolol for hypertension which was controlled.
On examination, he was fully conscious and haemodynamically stable with a pulse of 65 beats per minute and blood pressure of 105/72. Systemic examination was normal. Power was 3/5 in the right arm and leg with the right plantar reflex upgoing. There was progression of neurological signs 24 hours after admission, until the power was 0/5 in the affected limbs with mild slurring of speech 72 hours later. There was no evidence of fluctuating neurological signs. His higher mental functions were intact throughout his hospital admission. The electrocardiogram confirmed sinus rhythm at 60 beats per minute. The chest X-ray was unremarkable.
He was admitted and underwent an urgent computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain. The initial CT (Figure ) was performed 6 hours after the collapse. The hospital had access to a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner once a week and the next available slot was 6 days later. During the weekend following admission he was transferred to the stroke unit and reviewed twice daily. His neurological deficits deteriorated stepwise with 2/5 power in his right arm and leg at 36 hours progressing to 0/5 with mild slurring of speech around 72 hours post admission on Monday. There were no features suggestive of raised intracranial pressure. He had no altered sensorium. His case was discussed with the radiologist and the medical physician on call during the weekend. It was felt there was no need for an urgent repeat scan and all agreed the progression was likely to be due to the stroke. The radiologist reviewed the initial scan over the weekend and had no concerns about the calcified area, which was judged less likely to be a bleed, although this could not be ruled out. The decision was to perform a scan on Monday morning to confirm that the deterioration was due to the stroke and the suspected calcified area was not a bleed.
A repeat CT brain scan was performed after the weekend on the third day after admission (Figure ).

case_text:
A 65-years-old right-hand dominant woman presented to our unit with a 24-h history of a progressively worsening discoloration and swelling to her left index finger (LIF) associated with generalized swelling and tenderness of the left hand. She denied any recent trauma to her left hand. She gave a history of epilepsy due to multiple meningiomas for which she was maintained on dexamethasone treatment (4 mg/day) for 6 months.
Clinical examination revealed an afebrile, relatively well-looking woman, with classic cushingnoid appearance and a grossly normal neurological examination. Gross swelling to her left hand, most markedly to the LIF, was noted. Her LIF was cold, insensate and dusky with epidermolysis of the dorsal skin (). She also had ascending cellulitis extending to her elbow and palpable lymph nodes on her axilla. X-ray demonstrated gross soft tissue swelling but was otherwise unremarkable, with no signs of gas within the tissues. A clinical diagnosis of fulminant NF was made; she was admitted and empirically commenced on intravenous penicillin and booked emergently for debridement of her left hand. Her laboratory analysis revealed elevated C-reactive protein 560 mg/L and white blood cell count 24 × 109U/L and hyponatremia 128 mmol/L with a LRINEC score of 7.
Intraoperatively, the clinical diagnosis of NF was confirmed with circumferential necrosis of her LIF. The LIF was amputated at the metacarpophalangeal joint () and radical debridement was performed of nonviable skin and subcutaneous tissue on the dorsum of her left hand and distal forearm. The volar tissues and the proximal forearm demonstrated healthy bleeding skin and normal looking fascia. Postoperatively, she was managed in our high dependency unit for close monitoring. A second washout was performed 24 h later not revealing any further signs of infection. Microbiology cultures later revealed penicillin sensitive Streptococcus pyogenes species. Her wounds were resurfaced with a split thickness skin graft 2 days later (). She was subsequently discharged on Day 7 post presentation.

case_text:
The patient was a 34-year-old Japanese woman (gravida 1, para 1) whose previous personal and family medical histories were unremarkable. During this pregnancy, the patient's physical findings, cervical length, laboratory data, urinalyses, and fetal growth determinations were all within normal ranges; glucosuria or ketonuria was not detected.
At 23 weeks and 6 days of gestation, physical findings, fetal growth, cervical length, laboratory data, and urinalysis were all within normal range. Two days later, the patient thought she had caught a cold because of the onset of malaise and thirst. At 24 weeks and 3 days of gestation, she presented with complaints of nausea and lumbago. Upon examination, the fetal heartbeat and movement were positive. The physician on duty at the time of admission initially diagnosed the condition as poor physical condition due to the common cold. However, 5 h later, the patient went into labor, and the gestational sac and fetal head appeared, resulting in emergent hospitalization and a subsequent premature delivery.
Upon admission, the patient was 166 cm tall, weighing 72.7 kg (before pregnancy, 63 kg), and had a body temperature of 36.9°C and a blood pressure of 156/74 mmHg. A physical examination revealed labored breathing and cold extremities. A stillborn infant (592 g, female) was soon delivered. The associated blood loss was minimal, and uterine contraction was good; the placenta and umbilical cord (130 g) appeared normal. Soon after delivery, the patient's vitals were normal, apart from a blood pressure of 129/69 mmHg and a slight tachycardia, with a pulse of 113 beats/min. The patient had no lower abdominal pain but complained of epigastric pain.
The results of laboratory tests on blood collected during labor were examined () and confirmed an extreme hyperglycemia, with a blood glucose level of 950 mg/dL. Her urinary sugar and ketones were markedly elevated. The labored breathing observed during delivery became more severe, and the patient developed clouded consciousness, leading to management in the intensive care unit (ICU).
After admission, the patient's white blood cell count, serum amylase levels, blood urea nitrogen levels (BUN), and blood creatinine levels were elevated, leading to a diagnosis of sepsis, acute renal failure, and acute pancreatitis associated with diabetic acidosis. Following a diagnosis of coma due to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), acute renal failure, acute pancreatitis, and sepsis, insulin therapy (regular insulin, 7 U/h) and antimicrobial therapy (meropenem trihydrate) were initiated in conjunction with adequate hydration. The patient's laboratory findings and blood gas data improved with this treatment (), and she regained consciousness 24 h after admission to the ICU. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) was performed, revealing a CT severity index of 2 ().
Despite elevated postadmission blood glucose levels, the patient's glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels remained normal. However, C-peptide blood levels of 0.1 ng/mL indicated depleted insulin levels; antibodies against insulin, glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), and islet antigen-2 were not detected. Despite marked elevations of C-reactive protein and white blood cell levels, the patient's blood cultures were negative and she was afebrile. A search for factors contributing to DKA involved two investigations of possible viral infection (). The findings revealed elevated Coxsackie A9, B1, and B3 antibody titers. With the patient's consent, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing was performed; the findings showed HLA-DRB1∗0405-DQB1∗0401. The condition met all the diagnostic criteria of fulminant type 1 diabetes [] and was diagnosed as such.
The patient was discharged 13 days postpartum and her insulin levels remain depleted, 1 year later. The patient has required regular insulin (42 U/day) administration, with her blood glucose levels varying within the range of 150–250 mg/dL; occasional hypoglycemic episodes preclude higher insulin doses. The patient's HbA1c levels have recently been maintained at approximately 8%.

case_text: A 58-year-old woman with breast cancer presents to her primary care physician for referral to a medical oncologist. She denies any personal history of blood clots in her past. Her past medical history is significant for preeclampsia, hypertension, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and hypercholesterolemia. She currently smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day, drinks a glass of wine per day, and she currently denies any illicit drug use, despite a history of cocaine use. The vital signs include: temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 111/min and irregular, and respiratory rate 17/min. On physical examination, she has a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border, bilateral bibasilar crackles on the lungs, and a normal abdominal examination. At her follow-up with the oncologist, they subsequently plan to start the patient on a highly emetic chemotherapeutic regimen.

case_text:
A 45-year-old woman with a 3-year history of chronic anemia was followed up at the Gastroenterology outpatient department of another hospital, with a 6-month history of abdominal pain. The pain was intermittent, worse in the mornings, and localized to the epigastric region. The patient noticed that her abdomen became distended after meals and distension was relieved after a bowel movement. The patient noticed a 12-kg weight loss over the last 6 months. There was a history of nausea but no vomiting. The patient denied any history of loss of appetite, diarrhea or constipation, and upper or lower gastrointestinal bleeding. There was no significant past medical history other than anemia and multiple blood transfusions. The patient denied any history of tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, drug abuse, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, chronic renal failure, peptic ulcer disease, and chronic pancreatitis. Her family history was unremarkable. The patient did not have any prior surgeries or history of malignancy. Workup for her chronic anemia included CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous and oral contrast, which revealed duodenal intussusception. The patient was booked for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in the referral hospital but missed her appointment and asked for a referral to another hospital.
Upon arrival at our hospital, she appeared underweight (height, 162 cm; weight, 43 kg). Her vitals were stable, and she was afebrile (blood pressure, 118/67 mm/Hg; heart rate, 96 bpm; respiratory rate, 23 bpm; oxygen saturation, 98% in room air; temperature: 36.9 °C). On examination, her abdomen was soft and laxative, with no tenderness, or organomegaly. A complete blood count on the day of admission revealed the following: low hemoglobin level, 7.2 g/dL (12.0–17.0 g/dL); mean corpuscular volume (MCV), 78.0 fL (80.0–100.0 fL); low hematocrit, 24.8% (40.0%–51.0%); leukocyte count, 8.2 × 109/L (4.5-11.0 × 109/L); and platelet count, 323 × 109/L (150-450 × 109/L). Other laboratory profiles were unremarkable. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed significant dilation of the stomach with no detectable gastric lesion. The third part of the duodenum was distended by a sausage-shaped intraluminal structure with alternating fat planes and dilated vessels reaching up to the first part of the duodenum, suggesting retrograde jejuno-duodenal intussusception. There was no detectable soft tissue lesion, and the rest of the bowel was unremarkable (A–C). Endoscopic examination of the upper digestive tract revealed a large, long, mobile submucosal longitudinal and tortuous bulge extending from the first to the second part of the duodenum that moved freely with bowel contraction. The papilla of Vater was normal with no neoplastic process.
The patient underwent laparoscopic exploration, which revealed antiperistaltic intussusception in the proximal jejunum (). A jejunostomy was performed, and the mass was pulled through in the proximal jejunum (A).
A cholecystectomy was performed, and a pediatric feeding tube was passed through the cystic duct to locate the ampulla of Vater. The mass was not resectable without affecting the ampulla, so the decision was made to perform a pancreas-sparing duodenal resection. The excised duodenum with mass was sent for histopathological examination (B).
Pathological findings showed a large polypoid mass with the mucosa pedunculated from the bowel lumen, measuring 12 × 7.5 × 2.0 cm3. Microscopic examination revealed a bowel mucosa with underlying submucosa showing lobules of benign normal-appearing Brunner's glands separated by fibrous stroma. The nodular proliferation of Brunner glands was accompanied by cystically dilated ducts and adipose tissue with no microscopic features of malignancy (A–C). The patient was discharged postoperatively in good condition, given an appointment after 1 month.

case_text:
A 43-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of severe central chest pain, mild shortness of breath, and one episode of coughing up blood since waking up that morning. The pain worsens on inspiration, and she describes it as 8 out of 10 in intensity. Three months ago, she underwent a left modified radical mastectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 103/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 102/74 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. The left lower extremity is swollen and erythematous. Laboratory studies show a normal complete blood count, creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, and a creatinine clearance of 81 mL/min (N = 75–115). case_text: A 62-year-old woman with well-controlled type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis of both knees came to the outpatient urgent assessment area this morning because her left calf looked fuller and had become achy overnight after an otherwise uneventful day of light errands. Five weeks ago she underwent an elective total knee arthroplasty on that same side for end-stage degenerative joint disease; the operation lasted a little over two hours under general anesthesia, required two nights of inpatient recovery, and she was discharged home on postoperative day three with instructions for twice-daily walking exercises and formal physical therapy sessions three times weekly, all of which she reports completing faithfully. She ambulates independently with a cane only for longer distances, performs her own activities of daily living, sleeps in a regular bed, and specifically denies spending more than the normal nocturnal hours recumbent since surgery. Yesterday afternoon during a prolonged bout of stationary cycling at physical therapy she felt a sudden tight, pulling sensation from the popliteal fossa down the medial calf, which the therapist attributed to possible over-stretch of healing soft tissue; ice and elevation were applied, and the discomfort initially lessened. By dawn today she noticed the compression stocking on that limb felt snug and the calf was mildly tender to touch, prompting the current visit. She denies fever, chills, sweats, rash, insect bite, open wound, new varicose enlargement, or trauma beyond routine postoperative manipulation, and she has never experienced a clot in the legs or lungs. There is no chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, palpitations, abdominal pain, or neurologic deficit. Other history includes hypertension on lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and low-dose aspirin that her surgeon had asked her to discontinue one week before the arthroplasty but which she resumed two weeks ago; she takes no hormone replacement, corticosteroids, selective estrogen receptor modulators, or anticoagulants. Family history is negative for thrombotic or bleeding disorders, and she quit smoking twenty years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure; alcohol is limited to a glass of wine with Sunday dinner, and she denies illicit drug use. On arrival—before any analgesic or anticoagulant was given—vital signs were temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 134/78 mm Hg, heart rate 86 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. She transferred from chair to exam table using the cane but bearing weight fully on both legs. Cardiac examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmur, rub, or gallop; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and nontender with no organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities showed a well-healed midline knee scar with no erythema or drainage. The entire limb above the mid-calf looked symmetric to the contralateral side, but from the tibial tuberosity downward the operated calf appeared subtly fuller. A cloth tape placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 42.6 cm on the left and 39.1 cm on the right, a difference of 3.5 cm; mid-thigh girths measured 50.2 cm bilaterally, and ankle circumference around the malleoli differed by less than 0.5 cm. No network of straight or serpiginous subcutaneous veins was visible, and skin color remained uniform pink without brawny hyperpigmentation or streaking. Using the fingertips, gentle pressure along the course of the femoral vein in the groin, through the adductor canal, behind the knee, and down the posterior calf elicited a reproducible, focal “deep” soreness most pronounced halfway between popliteal crease and Achilles insertion; compressing the gastrocnemius muscle belly laterally produced only diffuse discomfort. The calf was neither excessively warm nor cool relative to the right side when compared with the dorsum of the examiner’s hand. Thumb indentation over the anterior tibial crest rebounded immediately without leaving a pit. Passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended increased the deep ache, whereas rotation of the hip and knee was painless, and straight-leg raise produced no radicular symptoms. Distal perfusion was intact: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill in all toes was under two seconds, and sensation to light touch and pinprick was preserved. Motor strength of ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion graded 5/5 on the unaffected side and 4+/5 on the operated side, limited mainly by discomfort rather than neurologic deficit. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was appreciated, and there was no knee effusion beyond expected postoperative fullness; a mild fluctuant collection along the medial incision was thought to represent early seroma rather than true joint swelling. Baseline laboratories drawn before any treatment showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelet count 276 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.1 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 seconds. A portable knee radiograph demonstrated appropriate prosthesis alignment and no peri-prosthetic lucency; ultrasound-compatible gel was not yet applied. Given the subacute onset of unilateral calf enlargement exceeding 3 cm, pinpoint tenderness traced along the deep venous path, and the recent major orthopedic surgery, intraluminal thrombosis remains a consideration; however, the abrupt pulling sensation during therapy and localized postoperative fluid collection raise the possibility of a gastrocnemius tear or seroma-associated inflammatory edema that may explain the findings as well or better. A compression duplex ultrasound from the common femoral vein to the ankle has therefore been requested on a stat basis while the patient rests in the observation bay without pharmacologic intervention pending imaging results.

The criteria for the Wells' Criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) score are listed below:

1. Active cancer (treatment or palliation within 6 months): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
2. Bedridden recently >3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
3. Calf swelling >3 cm compared to the other leg (measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
4. Collateral (nonvaricose) superficial veins present: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
5. Entire leg swollen: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
6. Localized tenderness along the deep venous system: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
7. Pitting edema, confined to symptomatic leg: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
8. Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
9. Previously documented DVT: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
10. Alternative diagnosis to DVT as likely or more likely: No = 0 points, Yes = -2 points

The total score is calculated by summing the points for each criterion.

case_text: A 59-year-old man was brought to the urgent access clinic by his spouse late this morning because the lower half of his right leg had become clearly larger and tight over the prior twenty-four hours after nearly a full week spent mostly in bed recovering from a febrile influenza-A infection that had left him too exhausted to do more than shuffle to the bathroom and back; he estimates he remained supine at least twenty-two hours per day from last Saturday through Wednesday evening before beginning to feel stronger yesterday. Earlier today, while dressing to leave the house for the first time since the illness began, he noticed his right pant leg clung snugly around the calf and that pulling on a walking shoe required more effort than on the left side. He reports no fall, twist, kick, or new exercise routine, denies insect bites, animal scratches, rashes, or local trauma, and has not traveled farther than the living-room sofa in ten days. He denies chest pain, pleuritic discomfort, dyspnea beyond a mild residual dry cough, hemoptysis, palpitations, syncope, fevers since Monday, chills, night sweats, abdominal pain, flank discomfort, dysuria, or recent weight change. He has never experienced a clot in the legs or lungs, never been told he carries a thrombophilia, and no first-degree relative has venous thromboembolism. His medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily, hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and allergic rhinitis treated seasonally with intranasal fluticasone; there is no chronic heart, liver, or kidney disease. He underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy nine years ago and a screening colonoscopy four years back, but has had no operations, invasive procedures, casts, splints, braces, or limb weakness in the past year. He does not take hormone replacement, corticosteroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants, stopped smoking twelve years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks two glasses of wine weekly, and denies illicit drug use. On arrival—before any medication or intravenous fluids were administered—he sat upright but kept the right knee extended on a pillow for comfort. Triage vitals read temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 130/78 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear to auscultation with only faint end-expiratory pops at the right base consistent with resolving viral pneumonia. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended with no hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities demonstrated a distinct bulge over the posteromedial aspect of the right calf accompanied by a lattice of dilated, straight, non-tortuous superficial veins functioning as collateral channels coursing from the mid-gastrocnemius toward the popliteal fossa, changes absent on the contralateral limb; skin temperature felt equal bilaterally and coloration remained normal pink with no erythema, hyperpigmentation, or stasis dermatitis. A flexible tape measure placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 42.0 cm on the symptomatic side versus 38.4 cm on the left, a difference of 3.6 cm; at mid-thigh the limbs were nearly identical at 54 cm, supporting localization of swelling to the calf rather than the entire leg. Thumb pressure maintained for five seconds over the anterior tibial crest produced immediate recoil without an indentation, mirroring the response on the left and indicating absence of pitting. Careful palpation along the femoral triangle, adductor canal, and popliteal fossa revealed no discrete tenderness or palpable cord; gastrocnemius and soleus bellies were supple, and passive ankle dorsiflexion elicited only a sense of tightness rather than sharp pain. Hip, knee, and ankle moved through full active and passive ranges without crepitus or effusion. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2+ and symmetric, capillary refill of the toes was under two seconds, and monofilament testing showed intact light-touch sensibility. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was detected, Achilles tendon was intact, and there was no posterior knee fullness to suggest a ruptured Baker cyst. Point-of-care labs obtained before any anticoagulant exposure revealed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 268 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 19 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 seconds. A resting 12-lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats/min without ST-T abnormalities. Portable anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the tibia and fibula ordered by his primary care physician earlier this morning showed intact bony structures and only soft-tissue prominence. No cellulitic erythema, myofascial herniation, tendinous rupture, lymphedema, or compartment syndrome signs were evident to account for the asymmetric calf enlargement. Given the objectively measured difference exceeding three centimeters, the visibly engorged superficial venous channels on the affected side, the recent five-day period of near-continuous recumbency, the lack of prior thrombotic episodes, absence of neurologic weakness or orthopedic immobilization, and the scarcity of any alternative musculoskeletal or infectious explanation on examination, a comprehensive duplex ultrasound of the right lower-extremity deep venous system has been ordered on an urgent basis while the patient remains under observation in the evaluation bay.

case_text: A 55-year-old man arrived to the urgent care bay late this morning because his left calf had become visibly larger and achy overnight, making it difficult to lace his cycling shoe and prompting concern during his commute to work. He recalled finishing a 40-mile recreational bike ride two evenings prior without mishap; after a routine cool-down he sat at his desk for several hours reviewing architectural drawings, noticing only a vague tightness behind the knee. On waking today he saw that the posterior calf looked fuller than its counterpart and felt a dull pressure that worsened when he planted the foot or flexed the knee, yet eased somewhat with the limb elevated on a pillow. He denies stumbling, muscle strain, insect bite, recent rash, fever, chills, sore throat, dental work, intravenous cannulation, or trauma to the limb. He has remained fully independent in activities of daily living, continues to commute by train and short walks, has not worn splints or casts, and reports no weakness or numbness of either leg. Past medical history consists of well-controlled hyperlipidemia managed with rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly; he has never been diagnosed with venous thromboembolism, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, chronic lung or kidney disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or connective-tissue disorder. His only surgical procedure was a laparoscopic appendectomy twelve years ago, and he has not undergone any operation, endoscopy, or invasive vascular study in the past year. Medications are limited to the statin and an over-the-counter fish-oil capsule; he does not use hormonal therapy, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants. He quit cigarette smoking twenty years ago after a 6-pack-year exposure, drinks one craft beer on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. There is no family history of premature myocardial infarction, stroke, known thrombophilia, or venous clot. Review of systems is negative for chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, palpitations, syncope, abdominal pain, flank pain, dysuria, leg sores, or weight loss. Before the administration of any medication or IV fluids, triage documented temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 124/74 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99 % on ambient air. The patient sat comfortably but kept the left leg slightly flexed at the knee. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with no organomegaly. Examination of the lower extremities showed focal enlargement restricted to the left calf; the thigh, ankle, and foot retained their usual contour. Using a cloth tape 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity, nursing staff measured 41.6 cm on the symptomatic side versus 37.8 cm on the right, a difference of 3.8 cm. Skin over the enlarged calf appeared mildly glossy but maintained normal coloration and temperature comparable to the contralateral limb; no serpiginous subcutaneous channels or dilated superficial veins were visible. Firm thumb pressure for five seconds over the anteromedial tibial surface produced a 3-mm depression that lingered approximately fifteen seconds before refilling, while identical pressure on the right produced immediate recoil. Systematic palpation along the path of the common femoral vein in the groin was unremarkable; however, pressing over the adductor canal, popliteal fossa, and posterior medial gastrocnemius elicited reproducible focal tenderness without a discernible cord. Passive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee extended provoked a pulling sensation but not sharp pain, and compression of the soleus bulk yielded no additional discomfort. Range of motion at the hip, knee, and ankle was otherwise full and painless. Distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill in all toes was under two seconds, and motor strength tested 5/5 in quadriceps, hamstrings, tibialis anterior, and gastrocnemius on both sides. Light-touch and vibration sensation remained intact, and no inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was detected. There was no knee effusion, posterior fossa mass, or Achilles rupture. A 12-lead ECG displayed normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with no ST-T abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula ordered by his primary doctor earlier in the day showed intact bony structures and only soft-tissue prominence. case_text: A 72-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a mild residual hemiparesis of the left lower extremity following a lacunar infarct thirteen months ago was brought to the emergency department by his daughter late this afternoon because he noticed that his right calf had grown noticeably larger during the preceding twenty-four hours. According to the daughter, the patient contracted a febrile bronchitic illness one week prior and, from Monday through Thursday, declined physical therapy sessions and remained in bed except for assisted transfers to a bedside commode; she estimates he was upright or ambulating less than ten minutes cumulatively on each of those four days. He began to feel better over the weekend, sat in a recliner for meals, and this morning attempted to shuffle down the hallway with his quad-cane when the pant leg felt tight against the mid-calf. He denies stumbling, twisting his knee or ankle, or sustaining direct trauma, insect bite, or animal scratch anywhere on the limb. There has been no flank pain, dysuria, fever recurrence, or chills, and he reports no chest pressure, new cough, dyspnea, palpitations, light-headedness, or syncope. He has never been treated for a clot in his legs or lungs, has not undergone orthopedic or abdominal procedures in the past year, and the only device on the left leg is an articulated ankle–foot orthosis worn intermittently for foot-drop related to the prior stroke; no casts, splints, or walking boots have ever been applied to the right side. Regular medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily, and simvastatin 40 mg nightly; he does not take estrogen products, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, corticosteroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants. He quit cigarette smoking twenty-five years ago after a 15-pack-year history, drinks a glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is notable for ischemic heart disease in both parents but lacks venous thromboembolism or known thrombophilia. Upon arrival—before analgesia, intravenous fluids, or antithrombotic therapy—the patient sat in a wheelchair with the right leg elevated on a pillow. Triage vitals were: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 138/76 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. He appeared comfortable, conversed clearly, and could move the paretic left limb only against gravity, whereas the right limb flexed and extended fully on command. Cardiac examination demonstrated a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen was soft and nontender with no hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities revealed symmetric thigh contours and ankle girths, but the mid-posterior compartment of the right calf was conspicuously fuller than its counterpart, and a faint lattice of straight bluish subcutaneous channels became evident after thirty seconds of dependency, emptying promptly with passive elevation. A flexible tape placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity measured 43.1 cm on the symptomatic side versus 39.0 cm on the contralateral calf, producing a difference of 4.1 cm; mid-thigh circumferences were 54.0 cm right and 53.8 cm left, and ankle circumferences at the malleolar level were 24.2 cm and 24.0 cm, respectively. The overlying skin was smooth, normothermic, and similar in color to the opposite limb without erythema, hyperpigmentation, ulceration, or stasis dermatitis. Capillary refill at all toes was under two seconds, and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally. Light-touch sensation remained intact throughout, and motor strength on the right side graded 5/5 at hip, knee, and ankle, whereas the chronically paretic left leg graded 3/5 in the same maneuvers. The examiner palpated joints and muscle bellies without detecting bony tenderness, crepitus, fluctuance, or calf firmness suggestive of compartment syndrome; the popliteal fossa was soft without a palpable mass. Straight-leg raise elicited no radicular pain, and passive dorsiflexion of the right ankle produced only a stretching sensation. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was noted. A bedside complete blood count drawn before any medication yielded hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, leukocytes 6.9 × 10⁹/L, and platelets 261 × 10⁹/L; basic metabolic panel showed sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, and glucose 156 mg/dL. Coagulation studies revealed an international normalized ratio of 1.0 and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 28 seconds. A twelve-lead ECG recorded normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats/min with no ST–T abnormalities, and a portable anteroposterior chest radiograph demonstrated clear lung fields. There was no erysipelas, cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, muscle tear, or overt lymphedema on examination that could more convincingly explain the unilateral calf enlargement accompanied by visibly engorged superficial veins in the context of recent prolonged bed rest and baseline left-side weakness, so the emergency team arranged urgent duplex ultrasonography of the entire right lower-extremity venous system while the patient remained hemodynamically stable and alert in the observation bay.

1. Active cancer (treatment or palliation within 6 months): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point

4. Collateral (nonvaricose) superficial veins present: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
5. Entire leg swollen: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
6. Localized tenderness along the deep venous system: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
7. Pitting edema, confined to symptomatic leg: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
8. Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
9. Previously documented DVT: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
10. Alternative diagnosis to DVT as likely or more likely: No = 0 points, Yes = -2 points

The total score is calculated by summing the points for each criterion.

case_text: A 62-year-old man is seen this afternoon in the ambulatory orthopedic suite immediately before a planned right knee arthroscopy with partial medial meniscectomy that the surgeon estimates will last under one hour under general anesthesia with a same-day discharge. He drove himself to the hospital, parked on the third deck of the garage, and walked briskly through the corridor without shortness of breath or assistance, stating that he still manages a daily two-mile neighborhood walk despite intermittent knee catching. His baseline activity is otherwise unrestricted; he mows his lawn, lifts groceries, and climbs the single flight of stairs to his bedroom several times a day. The knee problem developed after a low-energy twist six months ago and has been treated conservatively with physical therapy and NSAIDs; he has not required crutches, braces, off-loading boots, or any form of immobilization. Review of recent medical events confirms that he has not undergone any procedure, endoscopy, or hospitalization in the preceding four weeks, and the electronic record contains no admissions for systemic infection, chest infiltrate, or heart-failure decompensation during that period. His past medical history is notable for moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease related to a 40-pack-year cigarette exposure; he quit seven years ago and now uses tiotropium once daily and an albuterol metered-dose inhaler about twice a week before yard work, with no emergency-department visits or steroid tapers in the last year. Ten years earlier, after a transatlantic flight, he developed aching in the left calf and was found on duplex ultrasonography to have an occlusive thrombus in the popliteal and proximal posterior tibial veins; he completed a six-month course of warfarin with complete symptom resolution and has remained off anticoagulation since. He has never experienced sudden pleuritic chest pain or shortness of breath that prompted imaging for embolism, and surveillance CT scans performed for unrelated reasons have been devoid of pulmonary artery filling defects. There is no personal history of malignancy, myocardial infarction, stroke, inflammatory bowel disease, connective-tissue disorder, or hereditary bleeding or clotting syndromes, and he denies that any first-degree relative has suffered an unprovoked clot or been told of an inherited thrombophilia. Medications taken this morning include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled, lisinopril 10 mg daily for well-controlled hypertension, and a single 81 mg aspirin tablet, which he stopped two days ago per pre-operative instructions; he does not use hormone preparations, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs other than the aspirin. He drinks one beer with dinner on weekends, denies illicit substance use, and maintains a body mass index of 28 kg/m². On examination he sits comfortably on the gurney, conversing in full sentences. Vital signs recorded ten minutes ago show temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate 80 beats·min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, intact dentition, and full neck extension. Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated; S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung fields are clear to auscultation with faint end-expiratory wheeze that resolves after coached exhalation and no crackles. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Inspection of the lower extremities shows serpiginous, thin-walled superficial veins coursing up the medial aspects of both calves that become more prominent when he stands; the skin is warm, of equal color bilaterally, and free of edema or palpable cords, and calf circumferences measured 15 cm below the tibial tuberosity are symmetric. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are bounding and equal. Neurologic screening demonstrates full orientation and 5/5 strength throughout except for painful inhibition with resisted right knee flexion; sensation is intact. Only a single 20-gauge peripheral IV placed in the left forearm is present; he has never had a tunneled catheter, implanted port, or peripherally inserted central line. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn earlier today reveal hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, hematocrit 45 %, platelets 250 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.0 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 78 beats·min⁻¹ with no ST-segment changes, and a portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained for COPD surveillance last month demonstrates hyperinflated lungs without focal infiltrate, mass, or cardiomegaly. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided ninety minutes ago, and sequential calf compressors are at the bedside awaiting placement after induction; no pharmacologic prophylaxis has yet been administered while the anesthesia team finalizes the plan for laryngeal mask airway and multimodal analgesia.

case_text: An 88-year-old woman, a retired elementary school principal who still tutors neighborhood children in arithmetic twice a week, arrived to the internal-medicine clinic this morning for a comprehensive evaluation requested by her ophthalmologist before scheduling elective cataract extraction under monitored anesthesia. She walked from the parking lot without assistance but admitted that she now prefers using the building’s elevators rather than climbing more than one flight, citing limited endurance and a tendency to wheeze in cold air. The breathing limitation is familiar to her: she smoked one pack of cigarettes daily from age 18 until quitting 20 years ago and was told a decade ago, after spirometry performed during an influenza hospitalization, that her airways showed fixed obstruction that only partially improved with bronchodilator. Since that admission she inhales tiotropium 18 µg every morning, fluticasone–salmeterol 250/50 µg one blister twice daily, and keeps an albuterol metered-dose inhaler in her purse, using two puffs before climbing church choir loft stairs or when dusting high shelves; she has avoided emergency-department visits for the last two winters, has never required mechanical ventilation, and her most recent pulmonology note recorded an FEV1 of 1.3 L (56 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 and a diffusing capacity of 60 % predicted. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg swelling, or episodes of crushing substernal pain; reviews of prior electrocardiograms reveal normal intervals without pathologic Q waves, and serial cardiac enzyme sets drawn during two separate evaluations for atypical chest discomfort five and seven years ago remained below assay detection. Ten years previously her primary physician discovered fasting plasma glucose readings around 150 mg/dL on two separate mornings; she began metformin 1000 mg twice daily and attended diabetes-education classes at the local senior center. A hemoglobin A1c returned last week measured 7.1 %, and the logbook she carried shows pre-breakfast capillary values from 100 to 160 mg/dL. She endorses intact light-touch sensation in the toes, walks barefoot on carpet without imbalance, passes an annual dilated retinal exam with no hemorrhages or macular changes, and her urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio last month was 18 mg/g. Three years ago mildly elevated aminotransferase values—alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L—prompted abdominal ultrasonography that demonstrated a homogeneous but slightly echogenic liver measuring 15 cm with smooth capsule, patent portal flow, and no splenic enlargement; total bilirubin has remained 0.7–0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1, and she denies jaundice, pruritus, abdominal distention, variceal bleeding, confusion, or easy bruising. She consumes half a glass of sherry on holidays, avoids acetaminophen beyond 1 g per day, and takes no herbal supplements. Her renal indices drawn this morning reveal sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Lipid panel shows total cholesterol 184 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL, HDL 52 mg/dL, and triglycerides 132 mg/dL; she takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly without muscle aches. She never experienced sudden unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, or visual field loss and recounts completing the morning newspaper crossword in ink daily. Her daughter corroborates that household bills are paid on time and notes no personality change, wandering, or short-term memory lapses. Current medications also include aspirin 81 mg daily for vasculoprotection, calcium–vitamin D supplementation, and a nightly 5 mg zolpidem tablet for sleep maintenance; she is allergic to sulfonamide antibiotics, which once produced widespread urticaria. Review of systems is negative for melena, hematemesis, peptic discomfort, joint swelling, photosensitivity rashes, night sweats, weight loss, fevers, hematuria, or flank pain. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 126/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94 % on ambient air at rest, dropping to 91 % after a brisk 30-meter corridor walk, recovering to baseline within one minute. She appears well nourished with a body-mass index of 26 kg/m², speaks in full sentences, and does not use accessory muscles. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric, and pupils equal and reactive; oropharynx is clear without thrush. Neck is supple, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation is 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung examination discloses diminished breath sounds and scattered end-expiratory wheezes bilaterally with prolonged expiratory phase but no crackles or egophony. Percussion is hyper-resonant symmetrically, diaphragmatic excursion is limited to 3 cm, and tactile fremitus is reduced. Abdomen is flat, soft, with normal bowel tones; percussion yields a liver span of 9 cm, and the edge is smooth, palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, non-tender. There is no shifting dullness or fluid wave. Extremities are warm, radial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ bilaterally, no cyanosis, clubbing, or edema, and capillary refill is under two seconds. Neurologic assessment shows an alert, oriented woman with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength in all limbs, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady tandem gait; she completes serial sevens without error. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displays normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, axis within normal limits, no pathologic Q waves, ST-segment deviation, or conduction abnormalities. Portable chest radiograph shows a vertically oriented heart of normal size, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal airspace without focal infiltrates. She seeks counsel on whether her inhaled regimen is adequate for the perioperative period, strategies to keep blood glucose stable while fasting the morning of surgery, and timing of hepatology follow-up given her consistently mild enzyme elevations.

case_text: An 88-year-old woman, a retired elementary school principal who still tutors neighborhood children in arithmetic twice a week, arrived to the internal-medicine clinic this morning for a comprehensive evaluation requested by her ophthalmologist before scheduling elective cataract extraction under monitored anesthesia. She walked from the parking lot without assistance but admitted that she now prefers using the building’s elevators rather than climbing more than one flight, citing limited endurance and a tendency to wheeze in cold air. The breathing limitation is familiar to her: she smoked one pack of cigarettes daily from age 18 until quitting 20 years ago and was told a decade ago, after spirometry performed during an influenza hospitalization, that her airways showed fixed obstruction that only partially improved with bronchodilator. Since that admission she inhales tiotropium 18 µg every morning, fluticasone–salmeterol 250/50 µg one blister twice daily, and keeps an albuterol metered-dose inhaler in her purse, using two puffs before climbing church choir loft stairs or when dusting high shelves; she has avoided emergency-department visits for the last two winters, has never required mechanical ventilation, and her most recent pulmonology note recorded an FEV1 of 1.3 L (56 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 and a diffusing capacity of 60 % predicted. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg swelling, or episodes of crushing substernal pain; reviews of prior electrocardiograms reveal normal intervals without pathologic Q waves, and serial cardiac enzyme sets drawn during two separate evaluations for atypical chest discomfort five and seven years ago remained below assay detection. Ten years previously her primary physician discovered fasting plasma glucose readings around 150 mg/dL on two separate mornings; she began metformin 1000 mg twice daily and attended diabetes-education classes at the local senior center. A hemoglobin A1c returned last week measured 7.1 %, and the logbook she carried shows pre-breakfast capillary values from 100 to 160 mg/dL. She endorses intact light-touch sensation in the toes, walks barefoot on carpet without imbalance, passes an annual dilated retinal exam with no hemorrhages or macular changes, and her urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio last month was 18 mg/g. Three years ago mildly elevated aminotransferase values—alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L—prompted abdominal ultrasonography that demonstrated a homogeneous but slightly echogenic liver measuring 15 cm with smooth capsule, patent portal flow, and no splenic enlargement; total bilirubin has remained 0.7–0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1, and she denies jaundice, pruritus, abdominal distention, variceal bleeding, confusion, or easy bruising. She consumes half a glass of sherry on holidays, avoids acetaminophen beyond 1 g per day, and takes no herbal supplements. Her renal indices drawn this morning reveal sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Lipid panel shows total cholesterol 184 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL, HDL 52 mg/dL, and triglycerides 132 mg/dL; she takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly without muscle aches. She never experienced sudden unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, or visual field loss and recounts completing the morning newspaper crossword in ink daily. Her daughter corroborates that household bills are paid on time and notes no personality change, wandering, or short-term memory lapses. Current medications also include aspirin 81 mg daily for vasculoprotection, calcium–vitamin D supplementation, and a nightly 5 mg zolpidem tablet for sleep maintenance; she is allergic to sulfonamide antibiotics, which once produced widespread urticaria. Review of systems is negative for melena, hematemesis, peptic discomfort, joint swelling, photosensitivity rashes, night sweats, weight loss, fevers, hematuria, or flank pain. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 126/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94 % on ambient air at rest, dropping to 91 % after a brisk 30-meter corridor walk, recovering to baseline within one minute. She appears well nourished with a body-mass index of 26 kg/m², speaks in full sentences, and does not use accessory muscles. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric, and pupils equal and reactive; oropharynx is clear without thrush. Neck is supple, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation is 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung examination discloses diminished breath sounds and scattered end-expiratory wheezes bilaterally with prolonged expiratory phase but no crackles or egophony. Percussion is hyper-resonant symmetrically, diaphragmatic excursion is limited to 3 cm, and tactile fremitus is reduced. Abdomen is flat, soft, with normal bowel tones; percussion yields a liver span of 9 cm, and the edge is smooth, palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, non-tender. There is no shifting dullness or fluid wave. Extremities are warm, radial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ bilaterally, no cyanosis, clubbing, or edema, and capillary refill is under two seconds. Neurologic assessment shows an alert, oriented woman with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength in all limbs, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady tandem gait; she completes serial sevens without error. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displays normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, axis within normal limits, no pathologic Q waves, ST-segment deviation, or conduction abnormalities. Portable chest radiograph shows a vertically oriented heart of normal size, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal airspace without focal infiltrates. She seeks counsel on whether her inhaled regimen is adequate for the perioperative period, strategies to keep blood glucose stable while fasting the morning of surgery, and timing of hepatology follow-up given her consistently mild enzyme elevations.

1. Age: <50 years = 0 points, 50-59 years = +1 point, 60-69 years = +2 points, 70-79 years = +3 points, ≥80 years = +4 points
2. Myocardial infarction (history of definite or probable MI with EKG changes and/or enzyme changes): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
3. Congestive heart failure (CHF) (exertional or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, responsive to digitalis, diuretics, or afterload reducing agents): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
4. Peripheral vascular disease (intermittent claudication, past bypass for chronic arterial insufficiency, history of gangrene or acute arterial insufficiency, untreated thoracic or abdominal aneurysm ≥6 cm): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
5. Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or transient ischemic attack (TIA): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
6. Dementia (chronic cognitive deficit): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
7. Chronic pulmonary disease (CPD): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
8. Connective tissue disease: No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
9. Peptic ulcer disease (any history of treatment for ulcer disease or ulcer bleeding): No = 0 points, Yes = +1 point
10. Liver disease: None = 0 points, Mild = +1 point, Moderate to severe = +3 points
11. Diabetes mellitus: None or diet-controlled = 0 points, Uncomplicated = +1 point, End-organ damage = +2 points
12. Hemiplegia: No = 0 points, Yes = +2 points
13. Moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (CKD): No = 0 points, Yes = +2 points
14. Solid tumor: None = 0 points, Localized = +2 points, Metastatic = +6 points
15. Leukemia: No = 0 points, Yes = +2 points
16. Lymphoma: No = 0 points, Yes = +2 points
17. AIDS: No = 0 points, Yes = +6 points

The total score is calculated by summing the points for each criterion.

case_text: A 95-year-old widowed man who spent five decades touring the Midwest as a jazz pianist was brought to the university geriatric clinic by his niece this afternoon for a comprehensive evaluation before scheduling elective cataract surgery that the ophthalmologist believes will meaningfully improve his night vision for reading sheet music. According to the niece, he still lives alone in the ground-floor flat of a converted Victorian house and is keen on maintaining independence: he prepares oatmeal every morning, walks two blocks to a corner café for the newspaper, and practices scales on an upright piano for an hour daily. Over the past several winters he has noticed gradually worsening breathlessness when climbing the single flight to his bedroom, and neighbours occasionally hear him coughing low, hoarse rattles when the air is cold. He smoked unfiltered cigarettes while touring smoky clubs from age 18 until quitting at 70, estimating roughly 60 pack-years, and pulmonary notes from four months ago document post-bronchodilator spirometry with an FEV1 of 1.0 L (42 % predicted) and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.48, findings that prompted initiation of once-daily tiotropium 18 µg in addition to a longstanding budesonide-formoterol dry-powder inhaler taken twice each day; he keeps levalbuterol in a coat pocket, reporting use of two puffs most evenings after climbing the bedroom steps but no emergency-department visits or need for oral corticosteroids in the past year. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling, palpitations, chest heaviness radiating to the arm or jaw, or episodes of diaphoresis out of proportion to exertion, and serial electrocardiograms kept in an accordion file by his niece show normal sinus rhythm without pathologic Q waves. He has never been told he suffered a myocardial infarction, has never required hospitalization for congestive heart failure, and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed five years ago documented normal left-ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 60 %. Review of neurologic symptoms is likewise unremarkable: he completes the crossword in ink, balances a cheque book with single-entry accounting, recalls breakfast items without cueing, and has never experienced unilateral weakness, facial droop, slurred speech, sudden loss of vision, or transient language arrest. He likewise denies any physician-diagnosed stroke or transient ischemic attack. Twelve years ago an upper endoscopy performed after a bout of midnight melena revealed a 1.5-cm punched-out ulcer along the posterior duodenal wall with a visible vessel that required dual-clip placement; Helicobacter testing was positive, and he finished a clarithromycin-based triple regimen followed by eight weeks of proton-pump inhibition. Since then he has taken omeprazole 20 mg every morning and has not had recurrent bleeding, though he occasionally feels a dull epigastric gnaw that resolves with bland crackers. Endocrine records indicate type 2 diabetes diagnosed fifteen years ago during pre-operative labs for hip arthroplasty; he has since continued metformin 1000 mg twice daily and follows a loose carbohydrate-counting plan devised by a dietitian at the senior centre. Finger-stick logs the niece brought today show fasting glucose values ranging 95–155 mg/dL, and the most recent glycated haemoglobin measured 7.2 %. He denies blurred vision, burning plantar pain, ulcerations between toes, or episodes of severe hypoglycaemia; a retinal photograph taken last spring noted only mild background changes without macular oedema, and a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio was 22 mg/g. Serum creatinine repeated last week was 1.0 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 72 mL/min/1.73 m², with blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, and potassium 4.2 mmol/L. Liver chemistry panels have remained within reference limits for two decades—alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 80 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, international normalised ratio 1.0—and an abdominal ultrasound performed last year showed a smoothly contoured organ without steatosis, nodularity, or portal-flow abnormality; he has never exhibited jaundice, encephalopathy, ascites, or oesophageal varices and drinks a small glass of red wine only at Christmas. He refutes any history of malignancy, lymph-node enlargements, night sweats, or unintended weight loss and has never undergone chemotherapy or radiation. On review, the patient has peripheral vascular disease. An HIV antibody/antigen screen drawn during his hip surgery admission was non-reactive, and he reports no new risk factors since. Musculoskeletal review is notable only for mild morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal joints that eases after warm water, and there is no photosensitivity rash, oral ulceration, Raynaud phenomenon, or proximal muscle weakness. Current medications in addition to those mentioned include atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily suggested by his previous primary physician “for the heart,” calcium carbonate 500 mg twice a day, and vitamin D3 1000 IU; he reports a diffuse itchy rash to sulfonamide antibiotics in his forties and avoids that class. Today’s measured vitals: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/66 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 76 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 93 % on room air at rest, weight 64 kg, height 173 cm, body-mass index 21 kg/m². The patient sits upright, conversing in full sentences with occasional pursed-lip expiration; conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric. Neck is supple without carotid bruits, jugular venous pulsation is 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, and thyroid is normal in size. The point of maximal impulse is palpable in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are distinct, no murmurs, gallops, or rubs are audible. Lungs reveal diminished breath sounds bilaterally with scattered end-expiratory wheezes and prolonged expiration but no crackles. Percussion is hyper-resonant symmetrically. Abdomen is flat, soft, nontender, bowel sounds are present, liver span percusses 9 cm in the right mid-clavicular line, and there is no splenic tip or ascites. Rectal examination deferred at the patient’s request. Extremities are warm, radial, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+, capillary refill less than two seconds, no oedema, clubbing, or cyanosis. Neurologic screening shows an alert, oriented gentleman with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady though slightly wide-based gait aided by a wooden cane. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained on arrival demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 90 ms, axis within normal limits, and no ST-segment deviation. Portable chest radiograph shows hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and a vertically oriented heart without infiltrates. The patient wishes to understand whether his inhaled regimen needs adjustment before anaesthesia, whether continuing the proton-pump inhibitor will suffice to protect the prior duodenal lesion during peri-operative non-steroidal analgesics, and what fasting instructions can prevent glucose excursions on the morning of surgery.
