case_text: A 95-year-old widowed man who spent five decades touring the Midwest as a jazz pianist was brought to the university geriatric clinic by his niece this afternoon for a comprehensive evaluation before scheduling elective cataract surgery that the ophthalmologist believes will meaningfully improve his night vision for reading sheet music. According to the niece, he still lives alone in the ground-floor flat of a converted Victorian house and is keen on maintaining independence: he prepares oatmeal every morning, walks two blocks to a corner café for the newspaper, and practices scales on an upright piano for an hour daily. Over the past several winters he has noticed gradually worsening breathlessness when climbing the single flight to his bedroom, and neighbours occasionally hear him coughing low, hoarse rattles when the air is cold. He smoked unfiltered cigarettes while touring smoky clubs from age 18 until quitting at 70, estimating roughly 60 pack-years, and pulmonary notes from four months ago document post-bronchodilator spirometry with an FEV1 of 1.0 L (42 % predicted) and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.48, findings that prompted initiation of once-daily tiotropium 18 µg in addition to a longstanding budesonide-formoterol dry-powder inhaler taken twice each day; he keeps levalbuterol in a coat pocket, reporting use of two puffs most evenings after climbing the bedroom steps but no emergency-department visits or need for oral corticosteroids in the past year. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling, palpitations, chest heaviness radiating to the arm or jaw, or episodes of diaphoresis out of proportion to exertion, and serial electrocardiograms kept in an accordion file by his niece show normal sinus rhythm without pathologic Q waves. He has never been told he suffered a myocardial infarction, has never required hospitalization for congestive heart failure, and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed five years ago documented normal left-ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 60 %. Review of neurologic symptoms is likewise unremarkable: he completes the crossword in ink, balances a cheque book with single-entry accounting, recalls breakfast items without cueing, and has never experienced unilateral weakness, facial droop, slurred speech, sudden loss of vision, or transient language arrest. He likewise denies any physician-diagnosed stroke or transient ischemic attack. Twelve years ago an upper endoscopy performed after a bout of midnight melena revealed a 1.5-cm punched-out ulcer along the posterior duodenal wall with a visible vessel that required dual-clip placement; Helicobacter testing was positive, and he finished a clarithromycin-based triple regimen followed by eight weeks of proton-pump inhibition. Since then he has taken omeprazole 20 mg every morning and has not had recurrent bleeding, though he occasionally feels a dull epigastric gnaw that resolves with bland crackers. Endocrine records indicate type 2 diabetes diagnosed fifteen years ago during pre-operative labs for hip arthroplasty; he has since continued metformin 1000 mg twice daily and follows a loose carbohydrate-counting plan devised by a dietitian at the senior centre. Finger-stick logs the niece brought today show fasting glucose values ranging 95–155 mg/dL, and the most recent glycated haemoglobin measured 7.2 %. He denies blurred vision, burning plantar pain, ulcerations between toes, or episodes of severe hypoglycaemia; a retinal photograph taken last spring noted only mild background changes without macular oedema, and a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio was 22 mg/g. Serum creatinine repeated last week was 1.0 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 72 mL/min/1.73 m², with blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, and potassium 4.2 mmol/L. Liver chemistry panels have remained within reference limits for two decades—alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 80 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, international normalised ratio 1.0—and an abdominal ultrasound performed last year showed a smoothly contoured organ without steatosis, nodularity, or portal-flow abnormality; he has never exhibited jaundice, encephalopathy, ascites, or oesophageal varices and drinks a small glass of red wine only at Christmas. He refutes any history of malignancy, lymph-node enlargements, night sweats, or unintended weight loss and has never undergone chemotherapy or radiation. The patient's father has peripheral vascular disease. An HIV antibody/antigen screen drawn during his hip surgery admission was non-reactive, and he reports no new risk factors since. Musculoskeletal review is notable only for mild morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal joints that eases after warm water, and there is no photosensitivity rash, oral ulceration, Raynaud phenomenon, or proximal muscle weakness. Current medications in addition to those mentioned include atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily suggested by his previous primary physician “for the heart,” calcium carbonate 500 mg twice a day, and vitamin D3 1000 IU; he reports a diffuse itchy rash to sulfonamide antibiotics in his forties and avoids that class. Today’s measured vitals: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/66 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 76 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 93 % on room air at rest, weight 64 kg, height 173 cm, body-mass index 21 kg/m². The patient sits upright, conversing in full sentences with occasional pursed-lip expiration; conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric. Neck is supple without carotid bruits, jugular venous pulsation is 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, and thyroid is normal in size. The point of maximal impulse is palpable in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are distinct, no murmurs, gallops, or rubs are audible. Lungs reveal diminished breath sounds bilaterally with scattered end-expiratory wheezes and prolonged expiration but no crackles. Percussion is hyper-resonant symmetrically. Abdomen is flat, soft, nontender, bowel sounds are present, liver span percusses 9 cm in the right mid-clavicular line, and there is no splenic tip or ascites. Rectal examination deferred at the patient’s request. Extremities are warm, radial, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+, capillary refill less than two seconds, no oedema, clubbing, or cyanosis. Neurologic screening shows an alert, oriented gentleman with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady though slightly wide-based gait aided by a wooden cane. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained on arrival demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 90 ms, axis within normal limits, and no ST-segment deviation. Portable chest radiograph shows hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and a vertically oriented heart without infiltrates. The patient wishes to understand whether his inhaled regimen needs adjustment before anaesthesia, whether continuing the proton-pump inhibitor will suffice to protect the prior duodenal lesion during peri-operative non-steroidal analgesics, and what fasting instructions can prevent glucose excursions on the morning of surgery.
